γ(ρ).
Interpretation
Compatibility magnitude measures the quantity of surviving interoperability relations available for reconstruction.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.12.11 (Recovery Competition Theorem)
Recovery realization among competing trajectories is determined by recovery geometry rather than trajectory existence alone.
Proof
Suppose multiple trajectories
ρ₁, ρ₂, ..., ρₙ
possess compatibility intersections. Each trajectory is therefore recoverable. However recovery realization depends upon:
δᶜ, κ, v, β, ι, Φ, γ.
Trajectories possessing different geometric characteristics need not realize recovery simultaneously. Therefore trajectory existence alone is insufficient to determine recovery realization. Recovery realization is determined by recovery geometry.
QED
Interpretation
Recovery competition is fundamentally geometric. Not all recoverable trajectories are equally realizable.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.12.12 (Recovery Realization Functional)
The recovery realization functional is
ℱᴿ(ρ) = ℱ(δᶜ(ρ), κ(ρ), v(ρ), β(ρ), ι(ρ), Φ(ρ), γ(ρ))
Interpretation
Recovery realization is determined by multiple geometric quantities simultaneously.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.12.13 (Recovery Dominance Theorem)
Let
ρ₁
and
ρ₂
be competing recovery trajectories. Suppose
δᶜ(ρ₁) ≤ δᶜ(ρ₂)
κ(ρ₁) ≤ κ(ρ₂)
v(ρ₁) ≥ v(ρ₂)
β(ρ₁) ≥ β(ρ₂)
ι(ρ₁) ≥ ι(ρ₂)
Φ(ρ₁) ≤ Φ(ρ₂)
γ(ρ₁) ≥ γ(ρ₂)
with at least one strict inequality. Then
ℱᴿ(ρ₁)
ℱᴿ(ρ₂).
Proof
Each inequality weakly favors realization of ρ₁. At least one inequality strictly favors realization of ρ₁. Therefore the aggregate recovery realization potential of ρ₁ exceeds that of ρ₂. Hence
ℱᴿ(ρ₁)
ℱᴿ(ρ₂).
QED
Interpretation
Recovery competition becomes comparable geometrically.
Architectural Interpretation
The significance of the present theorem family is that recovery becomes a competitive geometric process. Recovery is no longer merely:
Uᴿ > 0 ⇒ Rec > 0.
Recovery now possesses:
trajectories,
compatibility intersections,
assembly complexity,
obstruction geometry,
basin stability,
realization competition.
The framework therefore transitions from existential recovery to dynamical recovery. Most importantly, recovery competition remains distinct from recovery selection. Competition identifies multiple recoverable trajectories. Selection emerges only through realization events. This distinction preserves the framework's commitment to constraint filtering rather than implicit optimization or arbitrary choice while still permitting formal analysis of recovery realization dynamics.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13 (Recovery Duality Architecture)
The preceding theorem family established recovery competition among multiple recovery trajectories. However, recovery competition does not imply recovery exclusivity. Multiple recovery trajectories may simultaneously intersect compatibility-bearing regions. The realization of one trajectory need not prevent realization of another. Consequently recovery admits a dual structure.
Recovery may proceed competitively through mutually exclusive utilization of compatibility-bearing structure. Recovery may also proceed cooperatively through shared utilization of compatibility-bearing structure. The present theorem family formalizes this duality.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.1 (Recovery Exclusivity)
Recovery exclusivity exists whenever realization of one recovery trajectory prevents realization of another recovery trajectory. Recovery exclusivity is denoted
Ξᴿ.
Interpretation
Competition requires exclusivity. Absent exclusivity, competition does not arise.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.2 (Shared Recovery)
Shared recovery exists whenever multiple recovery trajectories utilize common compatibility-bearing regions without preventing one another's realization. Shared recovery is denoted
Σᴿ.
Interpretation
Shared recovery is a cooperative recovery phenomenon.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.3 (Competition Necessity Theorem)
Recovery competition requires recovery exclusivity. Formally,
Compᴿ ⇒ Ξᴿ.
Proof
Suppose recovery competition exists. Competition concerns which recovery trajectory becomes realized. If realization of one trajectory does not affect realization of another trajectory, then no competitive determination is required. Consequently competition cannot arise. Therefore recovery competition requires recovery exclusivity. Hence
Compᴿ ⇒ Ξᴿ.
QED
Interpretation
Competition is not primitive. Competition emerges from exclusivity.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.4 (Nonexclusive Recovery Corollary)
Absence of recovery exclusivity eliminates recovery competition. Formally,
¬Ξᴿ ⇒ ¬Compᴿ.
Proof
Immediate from Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.3.
QED
Interpretation
Not all recovery intersections are competitive.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.5 (Shared Compatibility Theorem)
Compatibility-bearing regions may support multiple recovery trajectories simultaneously.
Proof
Compatibility-bearing regions are defined through surviving interoperability relations. The existence of one admissible interoperability relation does not generally eliminate other admissible interoperability relations. Therefore multiple recovery trajectories may utilize a common compatibility-bearing region. Hence compatibility-bearing regions may support shared recovery.
QED
Interpretation
Compatibility is not inherently rivalrous.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.6 (Shared Recovery Corollary)
Shared compatibility intersections imply the possibility of shared recovery.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.5, compatibility-bearing regions may support multiple recovery trajectories. Therefore multiple trajectories may realize recovery through a common compatibility intersection. Hence shared recovery is possible.
QED
Interpretation
Recovery need not be winner-take-all.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.7 (Recovery Assembly Theorem)
Shared recovery may generate larger organizational structures than isolated recovery.
Proof
Suppose multiple recovery trajectories intersect a common compatibility-bearing region. Each trajectory contributes interoperability-bearing interfaces. The shared compatibility region therefore contains a greater collection of admissible interoperability relations than any individual trajectory alone. Additional interoperability relations permit additional assembly possibilities. Consequently shared recovery may generate larger organizational structures than isolated recovery.
QED
Interpretation
Shared recovery is not merely coexistence. Shared recovery may be generative.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.8 (Structural Synthesis Corollary)
Shared compatibility intersections may induce synthesis of higher-order organizational structures.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.7, shared recovery increases available interoperability relations. The resulting interoperability network may support structures not realizable through isolated trajectories. Therefore higher-order synthesis may occur.
QED
Interpretation
Organizational structures may emerge through compatibility intersection itself.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.9 (Continuity Preservation Theorem)
Structural continuity may be preserved independently of realized structures.
Proof
Let
ℒᴬ
denote an admissible landscape. Let
Sᶜ
denote the compatibility landscape. Let
ρ
denote the collection of recovery relations. Suppose realized structures disappear. The admissibility relations defining
ℒᴬ
may nevertheless remain. The compatibility relations defining
Sᶜ
may nevertheless remain. The recovery relations defining
ρ
may nevertheless remain. These relations preserve the organizational geometry from which realized structures were previously assembled. Consequently the structural architecture remains recoverable. Therefore structural continuity may be preserved independently of realized structures.
QED
Interpretation
Continuity does not require preservation of realization. Continuity requires preservation of recovery-capable architecture.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.10 (Continuity Envelope)
A continuity envelope is the collection
𝓔ᶜ = (ℒᴬ, Sᶜ, ρ)
consisting of admissibility relations, compatibility relations, and recovery relations.
Interpretation
The continuity envelope preserves recovery-capable structure. Realized structures need not be preserved.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.11 (Recovery Reconstruction Theorem)
Realized structures may be reconstructed from a continuity envelope through recovery-realization mechanisms.
Proof
Suppose a continuity envelope
𝓔ᶜ
is preserved. The admissibility architecture remains available. The compatibility architecture remains available. The recovery architecture remains available. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.11.7, recovery reconstructs structure through compatibility-bearing interfaces. Therefore recovery-realization mechanisms may reassemble realized structures from the preserved architecture. Hence realized structures may be reconstructed from a continuity envelope.
QED
Interpretation
Recovery requires preservation of architecture rather than preservation of realization.
Architectural Interpretation
The significance of the present theorem family is that recovery acquires a dual character. Recovery may be:
competitive,
cooperative.
Competition requires exclusivity. Cooperation does not. The framework therefore rejects the assumption that recovery is inherently rivalrous. Compatibility-bearing regions may support multiple simultaneous recoveries and may even generate larger structures through shared interoperability. Furthermore, continuity localizes not to realized structures but to the admissibility, compatibility, and recovery relations capable of reconstructing those structures. The resulting continuity envelope
𝓔ᶜ = (ℒᴬ, Sᶜ, ρ)
preserves the geometry necessary for future recovery realization. Consequently continuity becomes an architectural property rather than a realization property.
3.13.13.A.222.13.12 Interface Composition Principle
Compatibility surfaces should not be regarded as indivisible organizational objects. Rather, compatibility surfaces are organizational assemblies generated by collections of interoperability-bearing interfaces. Consequently the organizational structure of a compatibility surface inherits from the structure of its constituent interfaces.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.13 (Interface Set)
Let
Z
be a compatibility surface. The interface set associated with Z is the collection
ℐ(Z)
of interoperability-bearing interfaces composing Z. Formally,
ℐ(Z) = {I₁, I₂, ..., Iₙ}
such that
Z = ⋃ Iᵢ.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces emerge from interface composition. Interfaces therefore constitute the elementary organizational structures of compatibility geometry.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.14 (Compatibility Surface Composition Theorem)
Every compatibility surface is generated by interface composition.
Proof
By Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.13,
Z
is constructed from the collection
ℐ(Z).
The compatibility surface therefore consists precisely of the interoperability-bearing interfaces comprising the surface. Hence compatibility surfaces are generated by interface composition.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces are organizational assemblies rather than primitive objects. The interface architecture is therefore more fundamental than the surface architecture.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.15 (Trajectory Utilization Subset)
Let
ρ
be a recovery trajectory intersecting compatibility surface Z. The trajectory utilization subset associated with ρ is
Uρ(Z) ⊆ ℐ(Z)
consisting of those interfaces utilized by ρ during realization.
Interpretation
Recovery trajectories need not utilize all interfaces within a compatibility surface. Different trajectories may utilize different interface subsets.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.16 (Partial Surface Utilization Theorem)
Recovery trajectories may realize through proper subsets of a compatibility surface.
Proof
Let
ℐ(Z) = {A, B, C, D}.
Suppose trajectory
ρ₁
utilizes
Uρ₁(Z) = {A, B, C}
while trajectory
ρ₂
utilizes
Uρ₂(Z) = {B, C, D}.
Both trajectories intersect Z. However,
Uρ₁(Z) ≠ Uρ₂(Z).
Therefore realization may occur through proper subsets of a compatibility surface.
QED.
Interpretation
Intersection with a compatibility surface does not uniquely determine utilization. Compatibility access and compatibility utilization remain distinct organizational quantities.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.17 (Shared Interface Theorem)
Distinct recovery trajectories may share interfaces while utilizing different interface subsets.
Proof
Using the notation of Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.16,
ρ₁
utilizes
{A, B, C}
and
ρ₂
utilizes
{B, C, D}.
Therefore
{B, C}
is shared by both trajectories. However,
A
belongs only to ρ₁, while
D
belongs only to ρ₂. Hence trajectories may simultaneously possess shared and non-shared interface utilization.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility participation need not be all-or-nothing. Interface utilization may overlap partially between trajectories.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.18 (Non-Exclusive Interface Utilization Theorem)
Shared interface utilization does not imply exclusive interface ownership.
Proof
Let
B ∈ ℐ(Z)
be utilized by trajectory
ρ₁.
The utilization of B by ρ₁ does not imply structural obstruction to utilization by additional trajectories. Consequently B may simultaneously participate in multiple utilization subsets. Therefore interface utilization is not necessarily exclusive.
QED.
Interpretation
Interfaces may be unidirectionally usable, bidirectionally usable, multidirectionally usable, or omnidirectionally usable. The applicability of an interface is determined by the structural conditions governing the interface rather than by utilization alone.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.19 (Recovery Assembly Theorem)
Recovery realization is an assembly phenomenon generated through interface utilization.
Proof
Let
ρ
be a recovery trajectory. Recovery realization requires intersection with a compatibility-bearing surface. However, realization is determined not merely by intersection with the surface but by the utilized interface subset
Uρ(Z).
Consequently the realized organizational structure depends upon the recovery trajectory and the utilized interface assembly. Therefore recovery realization is an assembly phenomenon generated through interface utilization.
QED.
Interpretation
Recovery realization is not simply
ρ ∩ Z.
Recovery realization is
Assembly(ρ, Uρ(Z)).
The compatibility surface provides interoperability resources. The recovery trajectory determines utilization. The realized organizational structure emerges from the resulting assembly.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.19.C1 (Distinct Assembly Corollary)
Distinct recovery trajectories intersecting the same compatibility surface may generate distinct realized structures.
Proof
Distinct trajectories may possess distinct utilization subsets. Distinct utilization subsets produce distinct assemblies. Therefore distinct realized structures may emerge from the same compatibility surface.
QED.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.19.C2 (Recovery Competition Corollary)
Recovery competition occurs among trajectories seeking realization through shared compatibility resources.
Proof
Distinct trajectories may depend upon overlapping interface subsets. Consequently realization opportunities may interact through shared interface utilization. Therefore recovery competition may arise among recovery trajectories.
QED.
Interpretation
Recovery competition is not competition between compatibility surfaces. Recovery competition is competition among recovery trajectories for assembly through compatibility-bearing interfaces.
Compatibility Consequence
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.12 through Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.19 establish the Interface Assembly Architecture. The resulting inheritance structure becomes
Interfaces → Compatibility Surfaces → Surface Intersection → Interface Utilization → Assembly → Recovery Realization
or symbolically
ℐ → Z → (ρ ∩ Z) → Uρ(Z) → Assembly → Rᴿ.
Consequently compatibility surfaces should be understood as interface assemblies rather than atomic compatibility objects. Recovery realization emerges through assembly from utilized interface subsets, permitting multiple trajectories to realize distinct organizational structures through the same compatibility surface while sharing, partially sharing, or independently utilizing its constituent interfaces. This architecture naturally introduces recovery competition, assembly diversity, and realization plurality within a common compatibility-bearing region.
3.13.13.A.222.13.20 Interface Realizability Principle
The interface architecture developed above is not an independent organizational construction. Rather, interface architectures emerge naturally from the constraint architectures governing interoperability.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces inherit their structure from interoperability relations. Interoperability relations inherit their structure from organizational constraints. Consequently compatibility surfaces inherit their structure from constraint architectures.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.21 (Constraint Localization Theorem)
Interoperability constraints localize to interface structures.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.9.1, interoperability exists whenever structural obstruction is absent. Structural obstruction is generated by constraint relations. Constraint relations do not act globally upon organizational structures as undifferentiated wholes. Rather, constraints apply to specific structural conditions. Consequently interoperability must be evaluated relative to the structural locations at which constraints act. Let such locations be denoted
I ∈ ℐ(Z).
These locations constitute interoperability-bearing interfaces. Therefore interoperability constraints localize to interface structures.
QED.
Interpretation
Interfaces arise because constraints act locally. Interoperability therefore inherits a local architecture. Compatibility surfaces inherit this locality through interface composition.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.22 (Nullstellensatz Interface Decomposition Theorem)
Compatibility surfaces admit interface decomposition.
Proof
The Nullstellensatz architecture establishes that admissible organizational structures are determined by constraint satisfaction. Consequently organizational structure is generated through collections of constraint relations. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.21, interoperability localizes to the structural locations upon which constraints act. Therefore any compatibility surface Z generated through obstruction-free interoperability may be expressed as a collection of interoperability-bearing interfaces
ℐ(Z).
Hence
Z = ⋃ Iᵢ
for
Iᵢ ∈ ℐ(Z).
Therefore compatibility surfaces admit interface decomposition.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces are not primitive objects. They are organizational geometries assembled from interface structures. This follows directly from the constraint-generated nature of admissible organizational structure.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.23 (Interface Inheritance Theorem)
Interfaces inherit admissibility from the constraint architecture.
Proof
Every interface belongs to a compatibility surface. Every compatibility surface belongs to the admissible landscape. The admissible landscape is generated by constraint satisfaction. Therefore every interface inherits admissibility from the governing constraint architecture.
QED.
Interpretation
Interfaces are not external additions to organizational structure. Interfaces inherit from the same admissibility architecture that generates organizational structure itself.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.24 (Interoperability Assembly Theorem)
Compatibility surfaces are assemblies of interoperability-bearing interfaces.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.22,
Z = ⋃ Iᵢ.
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.9.2, compatibility is equivalent to obstruction-free interoperability. Therefore each interface contributes interoperability structure to the compatibility surface. Consequently the compatibility surface emerges as an assembly of interoperability-bearing interfaces.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces should be understood as interoperability assemblies rather than compatibility objects. Compatibility emerges from the collective interoperability of constituent interfaces.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.25 (Partial Interface Utilization Theorem)
Recovery realization need not utilize all interfaces composing a compatibility surface.
Proof
Let
Z = {A,B,C,D}
be a compatibility surface. Suppose
Uρ₁(Z) = {A,B,C}
and
Uρ₂(Z) = {B,C,D}.
Then
Uρ₁(Z) ≠ Z
and
Uρ₂(Z) ≠ Z.
Therefore recovery realization may occur through proper interface subsets of the compatibility surface.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility access and compatibility utilization remain distinct organizational quantities. The existence of a compatibility surface does not imply complete utilization.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.26 (Interface Sharedness Theorem)
Interface utilization may be partially shared.
Proof
Using the notation of Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.25,
ρ₁
and
ρ₂
share
{B,C}.
However
A
belongs only to
ρ₁
and
D
belongs only to
ρ₂.
Therefore interface utilization may be partially shared.
QED.
Interpretation
Sharedness is an interface property rather than a surface property. Trajectories may share portions of a compatibility surface without sharing the entirety of the surface.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.27 (Omnidirectional Interface Theorem)
Interface sharedness does not imply interface exclusivity.
Proof
Let
I ∈ ℐ(Z).
The utilization of I by one trajectory does not imply obstruction to utilization by another trajectory. Whether additional utilization is possible depends solely upon the constraint conditions governing I. Therefore interfaces may be:
unidirectional,
bidirectional,
multidirectional,
or omnidirectional.
QED.
Interpretation
Interface applicability is determined by structural constraints rather than utilization history.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.28 (Recovery Assembly Realization Theorem)
Recovery realization is generated through interface assembly.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.11.17, recovery realization occurs through trajectory intersection with compatibility-bearing regions. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.24, compatibility-bearing regions are interface assemblies. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.25, trajectories utilize interface subsets rather than necessarily utilizing entire compatibility surfaces. Therefore recovery realization is generated through assembly from utilized interfaces. Formally,
Rᴿ = Assembly(ρ,Uρ(Z)).
QED.
Interpretation
The compatibility surface provides organizational resources. The recovery trajectory provides organizational direction. The utilized interface subset provides organizational assembly. The realized organizational structure emerges from the interaction of all three.
Compatibility Consequence
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.20 through Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.28 establish that the Interface Assembly Architecture is a direct consequence of the Framework's constraint architecture. The resulting inheritance chain becomes
Constraints → Admissibility → Structural Obstruction → Interoperability → Interfaces → Compatibility Surfaces → Interface Utilization → Recovery Assembly → Recovery Realization
or symbolically
ℂ → 𝒜 → Obs → I → ℐ → Z → Uρ(Z) → Assembly → Rᴿ.
Consequently the Interface Assembly Architecture is not an auxiliary extension of the Framework. It follows necessarily from the Nullstellensatz-derived admissibility architecture, the Interoperable Constraint Geometry architecture, the obstruction-based definition of interoperability, and the compatibility geometry developed throughout Chapters 3.12 and 3.13. Compatibility surfaces therefore inherit their structure from interfaces, interfaces inherit their structure from interoperability, and interoperability inherits its structure from the governing constraint architecture. This establishes the Interface Assembly Architecture as a formally justified extension of the Framework rather than an independent construction.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29 (Nullstellensatz Interface Emergence)
Let Z be a compatibility surface generated by admissible organizational structures satisfying a constraint architecture ℂ. Then Z admits decomposition into interface structures.
Proof
By the organizational Nullstellensatz architecture, admissible organizational structures are generated by satisfaction of constraint architectures. Let
ℂ = {c₁,c₂,...,cₙ}
be the governing constraint architecture. The admissible organizational landscape
𝒜
consists of structures satisfying the constraints of ℂ. Consequently every admissible organizational structure inherits its organizational geometry from the constraints generating it. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.9.1, interoperability exists precisely when structural obstruction is absent. Therefore compatibility-bearing organizational structures arise only where the governing constraints permit obstruction-free interoperability.
The existence of interoperability is therefore determined locally by the satisfaction of organizational constraints. Since constraints act upon particular structural conditions, interoperability cannot arise as an undifferentiated global property. Instead interoperability must arise through localized organizational structures at which the governing constraints permit organizational interaction. Let such localized structures be denoted
I₁,I₂,...,Iₖ.
These structures constitute interoperability-bearing interfaces. Consequently the compatibility surface admits decomposition
Z = ⋃ Iᵢ.
Therefore compatibility surfaces admit interface decomposition.
QED.
Interpretation
Interfaces are not introduced into the Framework. Interfaces emerge necessarily from the localized structure of constraint satisfaction. Compatibility surfaces therefore inherit internal structure from the same constraint architecture generating admissibility.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.30 Constraint Localization Theorem
Constraint-generated geometry necessarily possesses localized organizational structure.
Proof
Suppose organizational geometry were completely undifferentiated. Then all points of the geometry would be organizationally equivalent. In such a structure no meaningful distinction could exist between:
constraint satisfaction,
constraint violation,
interoperability,
or obstruction.
However, organizational geometry generated by constraints necessarily distinguishes among structural conditions. Therefore organizational geometry inherits localized structural features from the governing constraint architecture. Hence constraint-generated geometry necessarily possesses localized organizational structure.
QED.
Interpretation
Constraint geometry is inherently structured. The existence of local structure is therefore not an additional assumption. It is a consequence of constraint generation itself.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.13.30.C1 (Interface Necessity Corollary)
Every nontrivial compatibility surface possesses interface structure.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29, compatibility surfaces inherit localized organizational structure from constraint-generated interoperability. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.30, such localization is necessary. Therefore every nontrivial compatibility surface possesses interface structure.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces cannot remain structurally atomic.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.31 Interface–Interoperability Equivalence Theorem
Interfaces are precisely the localized carriers of interoperability.

By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29, interfaces emerge as the localized organizational structures through which interoperability is permitted by the governing constraints. By definition, interoperability exists wherever organizational interaction remains unobstructed. Consequently the interfaces generated by constraint localization are exactly the structures carrying interoperability. Therefore interfaces are the localized carriers of interoperability.
QED.

Interoperability does not float abstractly throughout organizational geometry. Interoperability is carried by interfaces.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.32 Nullstellensatz Interface Assembly Theorem
Recovery assembly is a direct consequence of constraint-generated interface structure.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29, compatibility surfaces decompose into interfaces. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.31, interfaces are localized carriers of interoperability. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.28, recovery realization is generated through assembly from utilized interfaces. Therefore recovery assembly occurs through organizational structures inherited from the original constraint architecture. Hence recovery assembly is a direct consequence of constraint-generated interface structure.
QED.
Interpretation
Recovery assembly is not an independent organizational mechanism. Recovery assembly inherits from:
constraints,
admissibility,
interoperability,
and interface localization.
The organizational structures assembled during recovery realization are therefore assembled from structures already present within the original constraint geometry.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.33 Nullstellensatz Recovery Realization Theorem
Recovery realization is a downstream manifestation of constraint geometry.
Proof
The organizational Nullstellensatz architecture generates admissible organizational structure through constraints. Constraint localization generates interfaces. Interfaces generate compatibility surfaces. Compatibility surfaces support interface utilization. Interface utilization supports recovery assembly. Recovery assembly produces recovery realization. Therefore recovery realization inherits from the original constraint architecture. Hence recovery realization is a downstream manifestation of constraint geometry.
QED.

Recovery realization is not external to the organizational Nullstellensatz architecture. Recovery realization is one of its later manifestations.
Compatibility Consequence
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29 through Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.33 establish that the Interface Assembly Architecture is not merely compatible with the Nullstellensatz architecture. Rather, the Interface Assembly Architecture is inherited from the Nullstellensatz architecture. The resulting inheritance chain becomes
ℂ → 𝒜 → Local Constraint Structure → Interfaces ℐ → Interoperability I → Compatibility Surfaces Z → Interface Utilization Uρ(Z) → Recovery Assembly → Recovery Realization
Consequently the organizational structures realized during recovery are assembled from interface structures whose existence is inherited from the same constraint architectures generating admissibility. Recovery realization therefore does not represent a departure from the Nullstellensatz foundation of the Framework. It represents a higher-order manifestation of the same constraint geometry viewed through the organizational architectures of interoperability, compatibility, assembly, and realization.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.34 (Nullstellensatz Foundation of ICG)
The preceding theorem family established that recovery realization inherits from interface assembly, interface assembly inherits from compatibility surfaces, compatibility surfaces inherit from interoperability, and interoperability inherits from the governing constraint architecture. The present theorem demonstrates that the organizational Framework itself is inherited directly from the original Nullstellensatz architecture. The objective is not merely to establish consistency between the Framework and the Nullstellensatz architecture. Rather, the objective is to demonstrate that the principal organizational structures of the Framework emerge necessarily from the mathematical structure of the Nullstellensatz itself.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.35 (Constraint Survival Theorem)
The fundamental object of the Nullstellensatz is the geometry of structures surviving a constraint architecture.
Proof
Let
k[x₁,...,xₙ]
be a polynomial ring over an algebraically closed field k. Let
I ⊆ k[x₁,...,xₙ]
be an ideal. The Nullstellensatz associates to I the variety
V(I)
defined by
V(I) = {p ∈ kⁿ : f(p)=0 for all f ∈ I}.
Consequently
V(I)
consists precisely of those structures satisfying all constraints represented by I. Therefore the fundamental geometric object of the Nullstellensatz is the collection of structures surviving the governing constraint architecture.
QED.
Interpretation
The Nullstellensatz is fundamentally a theory of constraint survival. The variety does not represent arbitrary structure. The variety represents surviving structure.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.36 (Organizational Survival Geometry)
Let
ℂ
be an organizational constraint architecture. The organizational survival geometry associated with ℂ is
𝒜 = {X : X satisfies ℂ}.
Interpretation
The admissible landscape of the Framework is the organizational analogue of the Nullstellensatz variety. Both are geometries generated by constraint satisfaction.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.37 (Admissibility Correspondence Theorem)
The admissible landscape is the organizational realization of Nullstellensatz survival geometry.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.35,
V(I)
contains precisely those structures satisfying the governing constraints. By Definition 3.13.13.A.222.13.36,
𝒜
contains precisely those organizational structures satisfying the governing organizational constraints. Both constructions are generated by identical logical operations:
constraint specification,
constraint satisfaction,
surviving structure generation.
Therefore the admissible landscape constitutes the organizational realization of Nullstellensatz survival geometry.
QED.
Interpretation
The Framework begins at the same mathematical location as the Nullstellensatz. Both begin with surviving structure.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.38 (Constraint-Generated Relational Structure Theorem)
Relations among surviving structures are inherited from the survival geometry itself.
Proof
Let
X,Y ∈ 𝒜.
Since X and Y belong to the survival geometry, both inherit the structural properties imposed by the governing constraint architecture. Consequently any organizational relation between X and Y must be evaluated within the geometry generated by those constraints. Therefore relational organizational structure is inherited from survival geometry.
QED.
Interpretation
Organizational relations are not external additions. They emerge within the surviving geometry.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.39 (Interoperability Emergence Theorem)
Interoperability emerges as a relation on surviving structures.
Proof
Let
X,Y ∈ 𝒜.
Admissibility establishes that X and Y survive the governing constraints. However admissibility alone does not determine whether X and Y may function together. A second relation must therefore distinguish:
obstruction-free coexistence,
obstructed coexistence.
By A.222.9, this distinction is precisely interoperability. Therefore interoperability emerges as a relation defined on surviving structures.
QED.
Interpretation
Interoperability is the first nontrivial relational structure arising from survival geometry.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.40 (Compatibility Emergence Theorem)
Compatibility emerges from obstruction-free interoperability.
Proof
By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.9.2, compatibility is equivalent to obstruction-free interoperability. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.39, interoperability emerges from relations among surviving structures. Therefore compatibility emerges from the obstruction-free relational structure of survival geometry.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility is inherited from survival geometry through interoperability.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.41 (Compatibility Surface Emergence Theorem)
Compatibility surfaces emerge as geometric regions of obstruction-free interoperability.
Proof
Compatibility relations partition the admissible landscape according to interoperability. The resulting interoperability-bearing regions constitute compatibility surfaces. Therefore compatibility surfaces emerge from compatibility relations.
QED.
Interpretation
Compatibility surfaces are geometric manifestations of obstruction-free interoperability.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.42 (Interface Localization Theorem)
Interfaces emerge from the local structure of compatibility geometry.
Proof

Therefore compatibility surfaces inherit local organizational structure. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.29, these localized structures are interfaces. Hence interfaces emerge from the local structure of compatibility geometry.
QED.

Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.43 (Recovery Assembly Emergence Theorem)
Recovery assembly emerges from interface utilization.

By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.41, compatibility geometry inherits from interoperability. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.39, interoperability inherits from survival geometry. Therefore recovery assembly inherits from survival geometry.
QED.
Interpretation
Recovery realization is not external to the Nullstellensatz architecture. Recovery realization inherits from the same constraint-survival structure generating admissibility.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.44 (Framework Inheritance Theorem)
The principal organizational architectures of the Framework are inherited from the Nullstellensatz architecture.
Proof
The preceding theorem family establishes the inheritance chain
I → V(I) → 𝒜 → Interoperability → Compatibility → Compatibility Surfaces → Interfaces → Recovery Assembly → Recovery Realization.
Each organizational architecture is derived from the preceding structure. Therefore the principal organizational architectures of the Framework inherit from the original Nullstellensatz architecture.
QED.
Interpretation
The Framework is not attached to the Nullstellensatz architecture. The Framework unfolds structures already latent within the Nullstellensatz architecture. The original Nullstellensatz question is:
"What survives the constraints?"
ICG progressively refines that question. At the level of admissibility:
"What organizational structures survive?"
At the level of interoperability:
"What surviving structures may function together?"
At the level of compatibility:
"What surviving structures may function together without obstruction?"
At the level of interfaces:
"Where is that interoperability localized?"
At the level of recovery assembly:
"What may be assembled from those interoperability-bearing structures?"
At the level of recovery realization:
"What organizational structures emerge from those assemblies?"
Compatibility Consequence
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.35 through Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.13.44 establish that ICG is a progressive unfolding of the original Nullstellensatz survival geometry. The resulting inheritance chain becomes
I → V(I) → 𝒜 → Obs → I → SC → Z → ℐ → Uρ(Z) → Assembly → Rᴿ
where
I = constraint ideal,
V(I) = survival geometry,
𝒜 = admissible landscape,
Obs = structural obstruction architecture,
I = interoperability architecture,
SC = compatibility relation,
Z = compatibility surface,
ℐ = interface architecture,
Uρ(Z) = interface utilization architecture,
Assembly = recovery assembly architecture,
Rᴿ = recovery realization architecture.
Consequently ICG does not depart from the mathematical structure of the Nullstellensatz. Rather, it develops successive layers of organizational structure already latent within the original constraint-survival geometry. Recovery realization therefore appears not as an external addition to the Nullstellensatz architecture but as one of its higher-order organizational manifestations.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14 (PNDS–Nullstellensatz–ICG Correspondence)
The preceding theorem families established that admissible landscapes, compatibility landscapes, recovery landscapes, and realization landscapes arise through the action of constraint systems upon candidate interoperability relations. However, constraint systems themselves presuppose the existence of a substrate upon which constraint partitioning may act.
The purpose of the present theorem family is to identify that substrate, to relate it to the Standing Algebra Σᴿ program, to establish its correspondence with the admissibility architecture of the Nullstellensatz, and to formally justify the necessity of substrate neutrality prior to domain-specific constraint application.
The central claim is not that admissibility generates the substrate. Nor is the central claim that compatibility generates the substrate. Rather, the substrate precedes admissibility, compatibility, recovery, realization, visibility, and obstruction. The admissibility, compatibility, recovery, realization, and obstruction architectures emerge only after constraint systems partition the relational possibilities present within the substrate. The present theorem family formalizes this architecture.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.14.1 (Pluralist Non-Domination Substrate)
The Pluralist Non-Domination Substrate, denoted
𝒮ᴾᴺᴰˢ,
is the domain-agnostic structural substrate instantiated by the invariants of Standing Algebra Σᴿ prior to any domain-specific interpretation. The currently identified PNDS invariants include:
standing preservation under admissible operations,
symmetry of equals (STC-5),
successor-consistent intervention,
bounded intervention,
rerunnable policy behavior,
directed repair,
bounded repair drift.
Interpretation
The PNDS is not generated through admissibility filtering. The PNDS exists prior to admissibility filtering. The PNDS is the substrate upon which admissibility architectures operate.
Definition 3.13.13.A.222.14.2 (Potential Relation Space)
The potential relation space associated with the PNDS is the collection of all candidate interoperability relations admissible within the substrate prior to application of domain-specific constraint systems. The potential relation space is denoted
𝓡₀.
Interpretation
𝓡₀ contains candidate interoperability relations. No admissibility partition has yet been applied. No compatibility partition has yet been applied. No obstruction partition has yet been applied.

𝓒
of domain-specific constraints acting upon
𝓡₀.
Interpretation
Domain constraints do not create the substrate. Domain constraints partition the relation space already present within the substrate.

𝓡₀

𝒮ᴾᴺᴰˢ.

Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14.7 (Substrate Neutrality Principle)
A universal substrate must remain free of domination relations prior to domain-specific constraint application. This is not a claim that the PNDS is universal but an observed characteristic necessary of any proposed universal substrate. 
Proof
Suppose domination exists within the substrate. Then at least one relation, interface, standing assignment, authority relation, or interoperability relation possesses privileged status prior to application of a domain-specific constraint system. Consequently the potential relation space
𝓡₀
contains structural asymmetry before constraint partitioning occurs. Therefore the resulting partition
𝒫𝓒(𝓡₀)

𝓒
but also upon the preexisting domination relation. Hence the resulting admissibility landscape is influenced by substrate bias. Therefore the resulting geometry is no longer determined solely by the domain constraint system. Consequently a dominated substrate cannot function as a universal neutral substrate.
QED
Interpretation
Substrate neutrality is a mathematical requirement. Without substrate neutrality, admissibility geometry inherits prior structural bias.
Corollary 3.13.13.A.222.14.8 (Invariant Necessity Corollary)
Violation of a PNDS invariant introduces potential substrate bias.
Proof
The currently identified PNDS invariants are precisely those conditions preserving substrate neutrality. Violation of such an invariant introduces privileged relational structure. By Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14.7, privileged relational structure introduces substrate bias. Therefore violation of a PNDS invariant introduces potential substrate bias.
QED
Interpretation
The currently identified PNDS invariants function as neutrality-preserving conditions.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14.9 (Nullstellensatz Admissibility Correspondence Theorem)
The admissibility architecture of the PNDS generalizes the admissibility architecture of the Nullstellensatz.

points satisfying the constraint system,
points failing the constraint system.
The resulting variety consists of the surviving admissible points. In the PNDS architecture, domain constraint systems partition potential relation space into:
surviving relations,
excluded relations.
The resulting admissible landscape consists of structures induced by surviving relations. Therefore both architectures arise through constraint-induced admissibility. The PNDS architecture generalizes the Nullstellensatz architecture by replacing candidate points with candidate interoperability relations.
QED
Interpretation
Nullstellensatz operates on candidate points. The PNDS architecture operates on candidate relations. The underlying admissibility architecture is shared.

Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14.22 (Universality–Domination Incompatibility Theorem)
A fully universal substrate cannot simultaneously contain domination relations, consequently, the PNDS cannot be universal.

Consequently some future admissible partitions become unavailable. This contradicts universality. Therefore a fully universal substrate cannot simultaneously contain domination relations.

3.13.13.A.222.14.28 (Universality Constraint Theorem)
Let ℛ denote raw relation space. Let 𝒞 denote the active constraint architecture. Let
PNDS ⊆ ℛ
denote the surviving relational substrate induced by the non-domination partition. Suppose U is a theory claiming universality. Then U must preserve the partition structure that generates PNDS. Formally,
Universal(U) ⇒ Preserves(U, PNDS).
Proof
The PNDS is defined as the surviving relational geometry generated by constraint filtering.  Thus
PNDS
{ρ ∈ ℛ : ρ satisfies 𝒞}.
Every realized structure inheriting from the PNDS is generated through relations contained within PNDS. Therefore all admissible organizational structures, recovery structures, compatibility structures, diversity structures, and resonance structures derive from PNDS-supported relations. Suppose a theory U claims universality. Then U must account for all admissible realizations. Since all admissible realizations inherit from PNDS, U must preserve the relational partition responsible for PNDS generation. Otherwise there exist PNDS-supported structures not represented by U. This contradicts universality. Therefore
Universal(U) ⇒ Preserves(U, PNDS).
QED
Interpretation
The theorem does not establish that the PNDS is a universal theory. The theorem establishes that any universal theory must preserve the partition architecture responsible for the PNDS. The burden is therefore shifted from demonstrating universal explanatory completeness to demonstrating preservation of substrate-generating structure.

Theorem A.222.14.29 (Universal Constraint Extraction Theorem)
Let Σ denote a structural invariant. Suppose Σ survives transport across multiple realization mechanisms while preserving compatibility architecture. Then Σ constitutes a candidate universal constraint. Formally,
∀Rᵢ ∈ Fᴿᴹ, Σ(Rᵢ)=Σ ⇒ CandidateUniversalConstraint(Σ).
Proof
The Realization Mechanism Frame was introduced to separate architectural truth from realization-dependent truth. Suppose Σ survives substitution of realization mechanisms. Then Σ is not dependent upon any particular realization. Its persistence must therefore arise from the underlying structural relations preserved across all realizations. Hence Σ represents an architecture-relative invariant. Any architecture-relative invariant that survives arbitrary realization substitution becomes a candidate constraint on universality. Therefore
∀Rᵢ, Σ(Rᵢ)=Σ ⇒ CandidateUniversalConstraint(Σ).
QED
Interpretation
The theorem does not prove universality. The theorem identifies a method for extracting necessary conditions that any universal theory would be required to preserve.

QED

Theorem A.222.14.30 (Inheritance Burden Theorem)
Let
K₀ ⇒ K₁ ⇒ K₂ ⇒ ⋯ ⇒ Kₙ
be an inheritance chain of architectural developments. Then successful invalidation of K₀ imposes a revalidation burden upon all dependent descendants. Formally,
¬K₀ ⇒ Burden(K₁,...,Kₙ).
Proof
Each descendant inherits some structural content from its predecessor.
If K₀ fails, inherited structures may no longer be justified.
Therefore each descendant must either:
Demonstrate independent validity, or
Demonstrate inheritance through an alternative chain.
Hence invalidation propagates a revalidation burden.
QED
Interpretation
This theorem formalizes the methodological role of inheritance throughout the treatise. The inheritance chain is not merely organizational. It allocates evidential burden.
Corollary A.222.14.30.1 (Survival Burden Corollary)
Repeated independent survival of the same invariant increases the burden upon competing explanations. Formally,
Multiplicity(Σ) ↑ ⇒ BurdenAlternativeExplanation(Σ) ↑.
Proof
Suppose Σ appears independently across multiple transported architectures. Then dismissal of Σ as a local artifact requires explanation of every occurrence. As occurrences increase, explanatory burden increases. Therefore
Multiplicity(Σ) ↑
implies
BurdenAlternativeExplanation(Σ) ↑.
QED
Interpretation
This corollary formalizes why recurring structures across Standing Algebra Σᴿ, Nullstellensatz, ICG, PNDS, Compatibility Geometry, Recovery Architecture, Diversity Geometry, Resonance Architecture, and Self-Localization Architecture are methodologically significant. The significance is not that recurrence proves universality. The significance is that recurrence increases the burden on any explanation that attempts to classify the recurrence as accidental.
Architectural Interpretation
The PNDS therefore establishes a critical distinction. The treatise does not claim the existence of a universal theory. The treatise derives structural conditions that any universal theory must preserve. The resulting implication is
Universal Theory ⇒ Constraint Filtering ⇒ PNDS ⇒ Compatibility Geometry ⇒ Recovery Geometry ⇒ Diversity Geometry ⇒ Localization Geometry
while avoiding the stronger and unjustified converse
PNDS ⇒ Universal Theory.
This distinction preserves methodological rigor while explaining why recurring structures appear throughout Standing Algebra Σᴿ, On Relevance, Nullstellensatz, ICG, the Compatibility Kernel, Recovery Architecture, Diversity Surface Geometry, Resonance Architecture, and Organizational Self-Localization. The recurrence is interpreted not as proof of universality but as evidence that the same substrate-level partition geometry is being repeatedly encountered from multiple architectural directions.
3.13.13.A.222.14.31 Invariant Consequence Extraction Architecture
The purpose of this architecture is to formalize the procedure by which structural invariants generate theorem families. The architecture is intended to convert structural persistence into reproducible consequence generation. The architecture therefore does not introduce a new invariant. Rather, it formalizes the method by which invariants are decomposed, transported, analyzed, and expanded into derived structures. The architecture applies to any structural invariant Σ arising within:
Standing Algebra Σᴿ
On Relevance
Nullstellensatz

PNDS

Future descendant architectures
Definition A.222.14.31.1 (Structural Invariant)
A structural invariant is a structure Σ whose truth value remains preserved under admissible realization-mechanism substitution. Formally,
∀Rᵢ,Rⱼ ∈ Fᴿᴹ, Preserve(Rᵢ,Rⱼ,Σ) ⇒ Σ(Rᵢ)=Σ(Rⱼ).
Interpretation
Structural invariants belong to architecture rather than realization.
Definition A.222.14.31.2 (Consequence Extraction)
Consequence extraction is the operation that derives all necessary structural implications of a given invariant. Formally,
CE(Σ) = {C : Σ ⇒ C}.
Interpretation
Consequence extraction identifies structures that must exist whenever Σ exists.
Definition A.222.14.31.3 (Architectural Completion)
An invariant Σ is architecturally complete relative to a framework F when all extractable consequences have been formally analyzed. Formally,
Complete(Σ,F) ⇔ ∀C ∈ CE(Σ), Formalized(C).
Interpretation
The objective of the Compatibility Kernel is architectural completion rather than theorem accumulation.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.14.31 (Invariant Consequence Extraction Theorem)
Let Σ be a structural invariant. Then every valid consequence of Σ may be generated through systematic application of decomposition, transport, compatibility analysis, obstruction analysis, recovery analysis, localization analysis, realization-mechanism substitution, and cross-domain portability. Formally,
CE(Σ) = CE₍D₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍T₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍C₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍Φ₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍R₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍SL₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍RM₎(Σ) ∪ CE₍CDPI₎(Σ).
Proof
Suppose Σ is a structural invariant. Any consequence of Σ must arise from one of the following categories.
Either:
It arises from the internal decomposition of Σ.
It arises from transport of Σ into another architecture.
It arises from compatibility relations involving Σ.
It arises from obstruction relations involving Σ.
It arises from recovery relations involving Σ.
It arises from localization relations involving Σ.
It arises from realization-mechanism substitution.
It arises from cross-domain transport.
These categories exhaust the currently identified structural operations available within the Compatibility Kernel. Therefore every extractable consequence belongs to at least one category. Hence
CE(Σ)
is equal to the union of all consequence classes generated through these operations.
QED
Interpretation
The theorem establishes the consequence-generation engine itself as a formal architectural object. The Compatibility Kernel therefore becomes a theorem-generation architecture rather than merely a theorem collection.
Definition A.222.14.31.4 (Decomposition Operator)
The decomposition operator is
𝒟ₑ.
For invariant Σ,
𝒟ₑ(Σ) = {σ₁,σ₂,...,σₙ}
such that
Σ
is realized through the interaction of
σ₁,...,σₙ.
Interpretation
Decomposition identifies constituent structures.
Definition A.222.14.31.5 (Transport Operator)
The transport operator is
𝒯.
For architectures
A
and
B, 𝒯ₐ→ᵦ(Σ)
maps Σ into B while preserving admissible structure.
Interpretation
Transport identifies portability.
Definition A.222.14.31.6 (Compatibility Operator)
The compatibility operator is
𝒞.
For invariant Σ,
𝒞(Σ) = {X : SC(Σ,X) > 0}.
Interpretation
Compatibility extraction identifies admissible interoperability.
Definition A.222.14.31.7 (Obstruction Operator)
The obstruction operator is
Φ.
For invariant Σ,
Φ(Σ) = {O : O obstructs realization of Σ}.
Interpretation
Obstruction extraction identifies realization barriers.
Definition A.222.14.31.8 (Recovery Operator)
The recovery operator is
Rec.
For invariant Σ,
Rec(Σ) = {ρ : ρ reconstructs realization after obstruction}.
Interpretation
Recovery extraction identifies persistence structures.
Definition A.222.14.31.9 (Localization Operator)
The localization operator is
SL.
For invariant Σ,
SL(Σ) = Position(Σ).
Interpretation
Localization identifies architectural location.
Definition A.222.14.31.10 (Realization-Mechanism Operator)
The realization-mechanism operator is
Fᴿᴹ.
For invariant Σ,
Fᴿᴹ(Σ) = {Σ(R₁),Σ(R₂),...,Σ(Rₙ)}.
Interpretation
The operator tests realization independence.
Definition A.222.14.31.11 (Cross-Domain Portability Operator)
The portability operator is
CDPI.
For invariant Σ,
CDPI(Σ) = {𝒯ₐ→ᵦ(Σ)}.
Interpretation
The operator tests survival across domains.
Corollary A.222.14.31.1 Consequence Completeness Corollary
Failure to apply one of the extraction operators risks omission of valid consequences. Formally,
¬Apply(Opᵢ) ⇒ PotentiallyIncomplete(CE(Σ)).
Proof
Each operator generates a distinct consequence class. Omission of an operator may omit its consequence class. Therefore consequence extraction may become incomplete.
QED
Corollary A.222.14.31.2 Architectural Reproducibility Corollary
The consequence extraction process is reproducible. Formally,
Input(Σ) ⇒ DeterministicOperatorSequence ⇒ CE(Σ).
Proof
The operators are structurally defined. Application of the same operators to the same invariant produces the same consequence classes. Therefore the process is reproducible.
QED
Corollary A.222.14.31.3 Discovery Engine Corollary
The Compatibility Kernel functions as a structural consequence-generation engine.
Proof
By Theorem A.222.14.31, consequences are generated through systematic application of extraction operators. Therefore the framework generates new theorem candidates from existing invariants. Hence the Compatibility Kernel functions as a consequence-generation engine.
QED
Architectural Interpretation
The preceding theorem family formalizes the methodology that has implicitly governed the development of Standing Algebra Σᴿ, Nullstellensatz, ICG, PNDS, Compatibility Geometry, Recovery Architecture, Diversity Geometry, Resonance Architecture, and Self-Localization Architecture. The process may be summarized as
Invariant ⇒ Decompose ⇒ Transport ⇒ Analyze Compatibility ⇒ Analyze Obstruction ⇒ Analyze Recovery ⇒ Analyze Localization ⇒ Apply Fᴿᴹ ⇒ Apply CDPI ⇒ Extract Consequences.
The framework therefore ceases to be merely a collection of results. It becomes a formally defined architectural engine whose purpose is to generate and exhaust the consequence space of structural invariants. Under this interpretation, the recurring structures throughout the treatises are not independent discoveries. They are outputs of a common consequence-extraction process acting repeatedly upon the same underlying substrate geometry.
Worked Example 3.13.13.A.222.14.31.4 (Predictive Obstruction Localization in a Fuse System)
The purpose of the present example is to demonstrate predictive obstruction localization through compatibility geometry. The example deliberately proceeds without assuming prior knowledge of the system failure location. Failure localization emerges through the interaction of:
interface geometry,
compatibility reserve,
obstruction geometry,
trajectory evolution.
The example therefore serves as the first explicit predictive application of the PNDS–Nullstellensatz–ICG architecture.
System Construction
Consider a system
Ω
consisting of:
a voltage source,
a conductor,
a fuse,
a load.
Define the interface surfaces
I₁ = Source ↔ Conductor
I₂ = Conductor ↔ Fuse
I₃ = Fuse ↔ Load
These interfaces constitute the interoperability-bearing surfaces of the system.
Compatibility Capacity Geometry
Suppose the interfaces possess interoperability capacities
Capacity(I₁) = 40
Capacity(I₂) = 15
Capacity(I₃) = 25
Assume the initial system current is
Current(0) = 12.
Definition (Compatibility Reserve)
The compatibility reserve associated with an interface is
γ(I,t) = Capacity(I) − Current(t)
Interpretation
Compatibility reserve measures remaining interoperability capacity.
Computation
At
t = 0
we obtain
γ(I₁,0) = 40 – 12 = 28
γ(I₂,0) = 15 – 12 = 3
γ(I₃,0) = 25 – 12 = 13
Interpretation
The interfaces possess different remaining interoperability reserves. No prediction has yet been made. Compatibility reserve alone does not determine failure.
Interoperability State Space
Let
σ(I,t)
denote the interoperability state associated with interface I.
For this example,
σ(I,t) = Current(t).
The compatibility regions become
𝒞(I₁) = {σ : σ < 40}
𝒞(I₂) = {σ : σ < 15}
𝒞(I₃) = {σ : σ < 25}
The corresponding obstruction boundaries are
∂Φ(I₁) = 40
∂Φ(I₂) = 15
∂Φ(I₃) = 25
Interpretation
Each obstruction boundary represents compatibility exhaustion for the corresponding interface.
Trajectory Construction
Suppose increasing environmental demand produces the trajectory
Current(t) = 12 + t.
The interoperability state therefore evolves as
σ(I,t) = 12 + t.
Compatibility Reserve Evolution
Substituting the trajectory yields
γ(I₁,t) = 40 − (12+t) = 28 − t
γ(I₂,t) = 15 − (12+t) = 3 − t
γ(I₃,t) = 25 − (12+t) = 13 − t
Interpretation
All interfaces lose compatibility reserve as current increases.
Obstruction Distance Construction
Define obstruction distance by
δΦ(I,t) = inf { d(σ(I,t),x) : x ∈ ∂Φ(I) }
For the present one-dimensional geometry:
δΦ(I,t) = ∂Φ(I) − σ(I,t)
Therefore
δΦ(I₁,t) = 40 − (12+t) = 28 − t
δΦ(I₂,t) = 15 − (12+t) = 3 − t
δΦ(I₃,t) = 25 − (12+t) = 13 − t
Interpretation
The fuse example is a special case in which
δΦ(I,t) = γ(I,t)
because:
the geometry is one-dimensional,
compatibility exhaustion defines obstruction,
trajectory velocity is constant.
This equality is not generally valid.
Obstruction Velocity
Define
vΦ(I,t) = − dδΦ(I,t)/dt
Computation yields
vΦ(I₁,t) = 1
vΦ(I₂,t) = 1
vΦ(I₃,t) = 1
Interpretation
All interfaces approach obstruction at the same rate. Consequently obstruction ordering is determined solely by obstruction distance.
Time-To-Obstruction
Obstruction occurs when
δΦ(I,t) = 1
For I₁:
28 − t = 0
τΦ(I₁) = 28
For I₂:
3 − t = 0
τΦ(I₂) = 3
For I₃:
13 − t = 0
τΦ(I₃) = 13
Therefore
τΦ(I₂)
τΦ(I₃)
τΦ(I₁)
Theorem (Predicted Failure Localization)
The first obstruction-bearing interface is
I₂.
Proof
By the First Obstruction Localization Theorem,
I* = arg min τΦ(I).
Since
τΦ(I₂) = 3
is minimal,
I₂
is the first interface intersecting obstruction geometry. Therefore
I₂
localizes failure.
QED
Prediction
Without invoking prior engineering knowledge, the framework predicts:
I₂ will reach obstruction first.
I₂ will become the first failure-bearing interface.
System failure will localize to I₂.
Comparison With Observed System Behavior
Now reveal the physical interpretation. I₂ is the fuse interface. The actual system behavior is:
the fuse fails first,
the remaining interfaces survive,
replacement of the fuse restores interoperability.
The predicted failure localization therefore agrees with the observed behavior.
Recovery Analysis
Following fuse replacement:
ρ
again intersects compatibility-bearing geometry. The source interface survives. The conductor interface survives. The load interface survives. Only the obstructed interface requires reconstruction. Consequently recovery occurs through restoration of a localized interoperability relation rather than reconstruction of the entire system.
Architectural Interpretation
This example demonstrates the complete predictive chain:
Interface Geometry
↓
Compatibility Reserve ( γ )
↓
Obstruction Distance (δΦ)
↓
Trajectory Evolution (ρ)
↓
Obstruction Velocity (vΦ)
↓
Time-To-Obstruction (τΦ)
↓
Failure Localization
The significance of the example is not that a fuse fails. The significance is that failure localization emerges from compatibility-obstruction geometry before the physical failure is revealed. This establishes the first explicit predictive obstruction-localization architecture and provides the mathematical foundation for the broader Predictive Obstruction Geometry developments of A.223.1–A.223.x, where obstruction localization will be applied to systems possessing nonlinear trajectories, multidimensional obstruction geometries, and competing recovery architectures.
3.13.13.A.222.14.31.6 Nonlinear Obstruction Geometry Example
The purpose of this example is to demonstrate a mathematically rigorous realization of trajectory geometry, failure geometry, and recovery geometry in which obstruction is not assumed to be linear. The example therefore extends the preceding trajectory architecture into a setting where local obstruction effects interact nonlinearly with connectivity structure. Unlike the previous illustrative example, all quantities are derived from graph structure itself rather than assigned as arbitrary values.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.1 (Admissible Relation Graph)
Let
G = (V,E)
be a finite graph. Let
V = {v₀,v₁,v₂,v₃,v₄,v₅,v₆}.
Let
E = { (v₀,v₁), (v₁,v₂), (v₂,v₃), (v₃,v₄), (v₂,v₅), (v₅,v₄), (v₄,v₆) }.
Interpretation
G represents the admissible relation structure surviving constraint filtering. For purposes of this example,
PNDS ≅ G.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.2 (Target Realization)
Define
Ω₀ = v₀
and
Ω* = v₆.
A realization trajectory is any admissible path from
v₀
to
v₆.
The graph therefore contains two candidate trajectories:
Τ₁ = (v₀,v₁,v₂,v₃,v₄,v₆)
Τ₂ = (v₀,v₁,v₂,v₅,v₄,v₆).
Definition A.222.14.31.6.3 (Admissible Connectivity)
Define admissible connectivity
κ(v)
by
κ(v)
deg(v),
the graph degree of vertex v. Computing degrees yields
κ(v₀)=1
κ(v₁)=2
κ(v₂)=3
κ(v₃)=2
κ(v₄)=3
κ(v₅)=2
κ(v₆)=1.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.4 (Nonlinear Obstruction Function)
Define obstruction geometry
Φ(v)
by
Φ(v)
1 ────── κ(v)
B(v)
where
B(v)
is a local obstruction term.
Interpretation
The first term arises entirely from graph structure. Lower connectivity produces larger obstruction. The second term represents local structural burden. For this example define
B(v₀)=0
B(v₁)=0
B(v₂)=0
B(v₃)=0.60
B(v₄)=0
B(v₅)=0.10
B(v₆)=0.
Computing obstruction yields
Φ(v₀)=1.00
Φ(v₁)=0.50
Φ(v₂)=0.333
Φ(v₃)=1.10
Φ(v₄)=0.333
Φ(v₅)=0.60
Φ(v₆)=1.00.
Remark
The obstruction geometry is nonlinear because
Φ(v)
depends reciprocally upon connectivity. Changes in degree do not produce proportional changes in obstruction.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.5 (Compatibility Function)
Define compatibility
γ(v)
by
γ(v)
log(1 + κ(v)).
Computing yields
γ(v₀)=0.693
γ(v₁)=1.099
γ(v₂)=1.386
γ(v₃)=1.099
γ(v₄)=1.386
γ(v₅)=1.099
γ(v₆)=0.693.
Interpretation
Compatibility increases with connectivity but exhibits diminishing returns. The logarithmic form prevents compatibility from growing linearly with degree.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.6 (Local Survivability)
Define local survivability
σ(v)
by
σ(v)
γ(v) − Φ(v).
Computing yields
σ(v₀)
−0.307
σ(v₁)
0.599
σ(v₂)
1.053
σ(v₃)
−0.001
σ(v₄)
1.053
σ(v₅)
0.499
σ(v₆)
−0.307.
Interpretation
Positive values indicate compatibility dominance. Negative values indicate obstruction dominance.
Theorem A.222.14.31.6.1 Trajectory Failure Localization Theorem
A trajectory fails at the first vertex satisfying
σ(v) ≤ 0.
Proof
Suppose
σ(v) > 0.
Then compatibility exceeds obstruction. The trajectory remains locally realizable. Suppose instead
σ(v) ≤ 0.
Then obstruction equals or exceeds compatibility. The compatibility surplus vanishes. Therefore realization cannot continue through that vertex. Hence the first such vertex localizes trajectory failure.
QED
Application
For
Τ₁ = (v₀,v₁,v₂,v₃,v₄,v₆)
the first non-positive survivability occurs at
v₃
since
σ(v₃)
−0.001.
Therefore
Failure(Τ₁)
v₃.
Theorem A.222.14.31.6.2 Distance-To-Failure Theorem
Define
δᶠ(Τ)
by
δᶠ(Τ)
min{σ(v): v ∈ Τ}.
Then
δᶠ(Τ)
is the structural bottleneck of the trajectory.
Proof
Every realization trajectory must pass through each vertex of the trajectory. The vertex possessing minimal survivability provides the smallest compatibility surplus available to the realization. Therefore no realization can exceed the limitations imposed by that vertex. Hence
δᶠ(Τ)
identifies the bottleneck.
QED
Application
For
Τ₁
we obtain
δᶠ(Τ₁)
−0.307.
The trajectory therefore contains structural failure.
Definition A.222.14.31.6.7 (Trajectory Horizon)
Define
H(Τ)
as the largest index k such that
σ(vᵢ) > 0
for every
1 ≤ i ≤ k.
Interpretation
H measures the extent of the trajectory that remains structurally viable.
Application
For
Τ₁
the trajectory remains viable through
v₂
but fails at
v₃.
Therefore
H(Τ₁)=2.
Theorem A.222.14.31.6.3 Recovery Diversion Theorem
Suppose an alternative trajectory avoids the first failure vertex. Then recovery remains admissible.
Proof
The graph contains an alternate route
Τ₂ = (v₀,v₁,v₂,v₅,v₄,v₆).
Computing survivability along the alternate route yields
σ(v₅)
0.4991
Thus the diversion bypasses
v₃
while remaining within the admissible relation graph. Therefore realization remains structurally admissible.
QED
Application
The original trajectory
Τ₁
fails at
v₃.
The alternate trajectory
Τ₂
avoids
v₃.
Consequently
Failure(Τ₁) ≠ Failure(Τ₂).
Corollary A.222.14.31.6.3.1 Pathway Failure Corollary
Failure of a trajectory does not imply failure of the realization objective.
Proof
The objective
Ω* = v₆
remains reachable through
Τ₂
despite failure of
Τ₁.
Therefore pathway failure does not imply objective failure.
QED
Architectural Interpretation
This example derives all quantities directly from graph structure. No survivability values were assumed in advance. Connectivity determines compatibility. Connectivity and local burden jointly determine obstruction. Compatibility and obstruction jointly determine survivability. Survivability determines horizon geometry, bottlenecks, and failure localization. The resulting inheritance chain is
G ⇒ PNDS ⇒ κ ⇒ {γ,Φ} ⇒ σ ⇒ {δᶠ,H} ⇒ Failure Localization ⇒ Recovery Diversion.
Unlike the earlier illustrative example, the obstruction geometry emerges from structural properties of the graph itself. The example therefore demonstrates a mathematically reproducible procedure in which compatibility geometry, obstruction geometry, trajectory geometry, and recovery geometry are all derived from a common relational substrate rather than imposed externally. This makes the example suitable as the first formal challenger-grade computation following Theorem A.222.14.31 because every quantity is generated from the underlying structure and the resulting recovery prediction follows from the mathematics rather than from assumptions about the outcome.
Theorem 3.13.13.A.222.15 (Frame Separation Architecture)
The purpose of the Frame Separation Architecture is to demonstrate that the recurring separation structures appearing throughout On Relevance, Standing Algebra Σᴿ, Nullstellensatz, Interoperability Constraint Geometry, Recovery Architecture, Diversity Architecture, Resonance Architecture, and the Compatibility Kernel are not independent domain-specific phenomena. Rather, they arise as inherited consequences of frame geometry itself. The objective is therefore to identify the minimal structural properties of a frame sufficient to generate the recurring separation architecture. The resulting theorem family seeks to establish that the following separations are not independent discoveries:
Potential ≠ Realization
Visibility ≠ Existence
Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure
Local Failure ≠ Global Failure
but instead emerge from a common generative architecture inherited from frame structure.
Dependency Chain
On Relevance
↓
Non-Domination Constraints
↓
Σᴿ Invariants
↓
PNDS Frame
↓
Constraint Partition Architecture
↓
ICG Relation Geometry
↓
Frame Separation Architecture
Interpretation
The dependency chain indicates that Frame Separation is not introduced as a primitive object. Rather, Frame Separation is inherited from the structure of the PNDS and the constraint partition that generates it.
Previously Earned Components
The following structures have already been established and may therefore be used without re-derivation.
From Nullstellensatz
Projection eliminates information. Projection residuals exist. Representability differs from existence. Formally,
Representable(X) ⇏ Existent(X)
and
Existent(X) ⇏ Representable(X).
From ICG
Admissibility exceeds realization. Compatibility exceeds accessibility. Surviving relation geometry exceeds realized relation geometry. Formally,
SC > 0 ⇏ Realized
and
Admissible ⇏ Accessible.
From Recovery Architecture
Pathway failure localizes. Objectives survive pathway failure. Recovery occurs through alternate trajectories. Formally,
Failure(Τ) ⇏ Failure(Objective).
From Visibility Architecture
Visible landscapes are proper substructures of existing landscapes. Formally,
Visible(ℒ) ⊆ ℒ.
The inclusion may be strict.
Definition A.222.15.1 (Frame Property Set)
A frame ℱ is said to possess the Frame Property Set if it satisfies the following properties.
F₁ (Non-Exhaustive Realization)
Realization does not exhaust admissible structure. Formally,
Realized(ℱ) ⊊ Admissible(ℱ).
F₂ (Non-Exhaustive Projection)
Projection does not exhaust existing structure. Formally,
Proj(ℱ) ⊊ Existent(ℱ).
F₃ (Relation Multiplicity)
Multiple relation architectures may support the same realized structure. Formally,
∃ρ₁ ≠ ρ₂
such that
Realize(ρ₁)
Realize(ρ₂).
F₄ (Local Obstruction)
Obstruction may localize to a proper subregion of a frame. Formally,
∃O ⊂ ℱ
such that
Obstructed(O)
while
¬Obstructed(ℱ).
Interpretation
The Frame Separation Architecture will be extracted entirely from these four properties. No additional assumptions will be introduced.
Lemma A.222.15.2 Non-Exhaustive Realization Lemma
If a frame satisfies F₁, then
Potential ≠ Realization.
Formally,
F₁ ⇒ Potential ≠ Realization.
Proof
Assume F₁. Then
Realized(ℱ) ⊊ Admissible(ℱ).
Therefore there exists
x
such that
x ∈ Admissible(ℱ)
but
x ∉ Realized(ℱ).
By definition, admissible but unrealized structures constitute potential structure. Hence
Potential(ℱ) Realization(ℱ) ≠ ∅.
Therefore potential and realization cannot be identical. Consequently,
Potential ≠ Realization.
QED
Interpretation
The separation
Tₚ ≠ Tᵣ
is therefore not an independent theorem. It is an inherited consequence of non-exhaustive realization.
Corollary A.222.15.2.1
Unrealized compatibility is a necessary consequence of F₁. Formally,
F₁ ⇒ Uᴿ ≥ 0.
Corollary A.222.15.2.2
Recovery architecture becomes admissible whenever unrealized compatibility survives. Formally,
Uᴿ > 0 ⇒ Rec > 0.
Corollary A.222.15.2.3 (Frame Occupancy Corollary)
Let
ℱ
be a frame. Let
ℛ
be a realization within
ℱ.
Then realization constitutes occupancy of admissible frame geometry rather than identification with admissible frame geometry. Formally,
ℛ ⊆ ℱ.
Proof
A frame is defined by its invariants. The invariants induce an admissible geometry consisting of all configurations satisfying the frame conditions. A realization consists of a particular instantiated configuration within that admissible geometry. Consequently realization occupies a region of admissible frame geometry rather than constituting the admissible geometry itself. Therefore
ℛ ⊆ ℱ.
QED
Interpretation
Potential and realization are distinct categories of object. Potential refers to the admissible geometry induced by the frame. Realization refers to occupancy within that geometry. Consequently the statement
Potential = Realization
cannot generally hold whenever the frame admits more than one admissible configuration. The separation therefore arises from the distinction between geometry and occupancy rather than from failure to realize available structure.
Corollary A.222.15.2.2 (Frame Relative Potential Corollary)
Potential is frame-relative.
Proof
A frame is defined by a collection of invariants. These invariants determine the admissible geometry associated with the frame. Potential consists of admissible configurations belonging to that geometry. Therefore potential is defined relative to the frame inducing the admissible geometry.
QED
Interpretation
Potential is not an absolute quantity. Potential is measured relative to the admissible geometry of a particular frame. Consequently complete realization relative to one frame does not imply complete realization relative to another frame.
Lemma A.222.15.3 Non-Exhaustive Projection Lemma
If a frame satisfies F₂, then
Visibility ≠ Existence.
Formally,
F₂ ⇒ Visibility ≠ Existence.
Proof
Assume F₂. Then
Proj(ℱ) ⊊ Existent(ℱ).
Therefore there exists
x
such that
x ∈ Existent(ℱ)
but
x ∉ Proj(ℱ).
Projection determines visibility. Therefore
x
exists while remaining invisible under the projection. Hence
Visibility ≠ Existence.
QED
Interpretation
This result inherits directly from Nullstellensatz projection geometry. Projection removes information. Existence therefore strictly exceeds visibility.
Corollary A.222.15.3.1
Hidden compatibility becomes possible. Formally,
∃SC
such that
SC ∉ Visible(ℱ).
Corollary A.222.15.3.2
Hidden diversity becomes possible. Formally,
∃𝒟
such that
𝒟 ∉ Visible(ℱ).
Lemma A.222.15.4 Relation Multiplicity Lemma
If a frame satisfies F₃, then
Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure.
Formally,
F₃ ⇒ Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure.
Proof
Assume F₃. Then there exist
ρ₁ ≠ ρ₂
such that
Realize(ρ₁)
Realize(ρ₂).
Suppose ρ₁ fails. Since ρ₂ remains distinct and realizes the same objective, the objective remains realizable despite pathway failure. Therefore failure of ρ₁ does not imply failure of the objective. Hence
Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure.
QED
Interpretation
Recovery Architecture becomes a necessary consequence of relation multiplicity. The existence of multiple admissible relation structures guarantees the possibility of pathway substitution.
Corollary A.222.15.4.1
Recovery trajectories are inherited from relation multiplicity. Formally,
F₃ ⇒ ∃Τ₁ ≠ Τ₂.
Corollary A.222.15.4.2
Objective reachability exceeds pathway reachability. Formally,
Reachable(Objective) ⇏ Reachable(Pathway).
Lemma A.222.15.5 Local Obstruction Lemma
If a frame satisfies F₄, then
Local Failure ≠ Global Failure.
Formally,
F₄ ⇒ Local Failure ≠ Global Failure.
Proof
Assume F₄. Then there exists
O ⊂ ℱ
such that
Obstructed(O)
while
¬Obstructed(ℱ).
Therefore failure occurs within a proper subregion of the frame. The remaining frame remains unobstructed. Hence local failure does not imply global failure. Therefore
Local Failure ≠ Global Failure.
QED
Interpretation
Obstruction localizes. The entire frame need not fail when a local compatibility surface fails.
Corollary A.222.15.5.1
Interface localization becomes possible.
Corollary A.222.15.5.2
Recovery basins may survive local obstruction.
Corollary A.222.15.5.3
Compatibility surfaces and obstruction surfaces become dual local geometries.
Theorem A.222.15.6 (Frame Separation Theorem)
Let
ℱ
be a frame satisfying
F₁, F₂, F₃, F₄.
Then the Separation Architecture necessarily emerges. Specifically,
Potential ≠ Realization
Visibility ≠ Existence
Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure
Local Failure ≠ Global Failure.
Proof
By Lemma A.222.15.2,
F₁ ⇒ Potential ≠ Realization.
By Lemma A.222.15.3,
F₂ ⇒ Visibility ≠ Existence.
By Lemma A.222.15.4,
F₃ ⇒ Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure.
By Lemma A.222.15.5,
F₄ ⇒ Local Failure ≠ Global Failure.
Combining these implications yields
(F₁ ∧ F₂ ∧ F₃ ∧ F₄) ⇒ { Potential ≠ Realization, Visibility ≠ Existence, Pathway Failure ≠ Objective Failure, Local Failure ≠ Global Failure }.
Therefore the Separation Architecture necessarily emerges from the Frame Property Set.
QED
Interpretation
The theorem demonstrates that the recurring separations observed throughout the corpus are not independent discoveries. They are inherited consequences of frame geometry. The same four frame properties generate the same separations regardless of realization mechanism, domain vocabulary, organizational interpretation, algebraic interpretation, or geometric interpretation.
Corollary A.222.15.6.1 CDPI Separation Corollary
The separation architecture is realization-mechanism neutral.
Proof
The proof depends only upon
F₁–F₄.
No realization-specific assumptions were used. Therefore the resulting separations survive admissible realization substitution. Hence the architecture satisfies CDPI.
QED

Recurring appearances of the separation architecture across domains are expected.

QED
Open Question A.222.15.Q1

At present, necessity of the four properties for the derived separations has been stablished relative to the existing architecture. However, sufficiency beyond the presently extracted separation family remains an open question. Future developments should therefore treat

as the current generating kernel of the Separation Architecture while remaining open to the discovery of additional frame-generating properties through the consequence-extraction engine.
Architectural Interpretation
Frame Separation is not a domain theorem. Frame Separation is a substrate theorem. The recurrence of

throughout On Relevance, Σᴿ, Nullstellensatz, ICG, Recovery Architecture, Diversity Geometry, Resonance Architecture, and compatibility is therefore explained by inheritance from the same frame-generating properties.
