3.14.7.14 Governance, Authorization, and Safety 
Computational capability does not confer authority. ICG may diagnose, forecast, filter, or recommend only within an explicitly authorized decision process. Automated intervention is not implied. Privacy, consent, contestability, review, and viable appeal or exit are required where applicable. Measurement must not reproduce domination through inaccessible categories or unreviewable models. 
Theorem 3.14.7.18 (Measurement–Computation Sufficiency Theorem) 
For declared task τ, computational ICG is operationally sufficient only if jointly supplied with a valid observation model; operational definitions; identifiable or equivalence-qualified estimands; calibrated estimators; uncertainty propagation; type-valid representations; cross-projection consistency; terminating or error-bounded algorithms; validated decision criteria; reproducible provenance; and authorized governance. 
Proof 
Each condition blocks a distinct failure mode: ungrounded observation, undefined construct, non-identifiability, estimation error, false precision, invalid type substitution, architectural contradiction, uncontrolled computation, undefined optimization, irreproducibility, or unauthorized action. Omission permits an unjustified output. Sufficiency remains task-relative. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
No single dataset makes ICG universally operational. The theorem defines the dependency chain a deployment must satisfy. 
3.14.7.15 Application to the Organizational Demonstration 
A real study requires consented, provenance-preserved measurements of communication, dependencies, decisions, participation, outcomes, interventions, and temporal transitions. These would estimate candidate architectures, test Uᴿ > 0, locate transition bands, evaluate resonance through aligned response, quantify pressure and representation with uncertainty, and compare interventions prospectively. No numerical result is supplied because no measured organizational dataset was provided; no values have been fabricated. 
3.14.7.16 Concluding Architecture 
The full computational chain is 
Observed records → measurement model → candidate architectures → identifiability analysis → estimation with uncertainty → cross-projection consistency → trajectory generation → admissibility filtering → nondominated landscape → prospective validation → authorized action.
Measurement and Computational ICG does not replace established statistical, causal, dynamical, spectral, or optimization methods. It requires their outputs to remain coordinated within one constraint-generated transition architecture and every operational conclusion to remain traceable, uncertainty-qualified, empirically tested, and realization-mechanism-neutral where warranted. ICG is now computationally specifiable; it becomes empirically credible only when a deployment satisfies these requirements. 
3.14.8 Computational Realization Demonstration Architecture 
3.14.8.1 Purpose, Scope, and Realization Status 
Sections 3.14.5–3.14.7 established interoperability unification, comparative capability, and the measurement–computation dependency chain. The present section supplies a concrete computational realization of the same organizational demonstration. Its purpose is not to assert that software is the architecture, nor to claim that one programming language is mathematically privileged. The code is an executable specification: a realization mechanism whose objects, types, invariants, and transformations are required to correspond to mathematical structures already defined. 
Under the Realization Mechanism Frame Fᴿᴹ, the architectural object and its software realization remain distinct. Architectural validity is established in the mathematics. Computational validity requires faithful implementation of that mathematics. Empirical validity additionally requires measured data, calibration, uncertainty analysis, and validation. None of these levels may be substituted for another. 
Architecture → specification → software realization → empirical instantiation
The code below is valid Python 3 source intended for close reading. It is not executed within the treatise, does not contain fabricated organizational measurements, and does not produce numerical claims. Domain values enter only through validated records supplied by a future empirical study. 
3.14.8.2 Implementation Contract 
The implementation contract states the conditions under which a program may be called an ICG realization. 
Every software type must correspond to a defined mathematical type. 
Every computed quantity must identify its estimator, unit, uncertainty, and provenance. 
Every latent quantity must remain distinguishable from an observation. 
Every reconstruction must return a family or equivalence class unless injectivity is proved. 
Every trajectory must be filtered by all declared admissibility conditions before ranking. 
The word best is prohibited unless an ordering rule is explicitly supplied. 
Failure of a pathway must not be identified with failure of its objective. 
A structural-recovery claim must test the governing obstruction rather than outcome improvement alone. 
No automated action is authorized merely because a computation returns a recommendation. 
Definition 3.14.8.1 (Computational Realization Map) 
Let 𝒜 be the mathematical architecture and 𝒞 a computational type system. A computational realization map is a partial map 
ρᶜ : 𝒜 ⇀ 𝒞
that assigns each implemented architectural object a typed computational representative while preserving every invariant required by the operation being implemented. Partiality is intentional: an implementation need not realize every object, but it must not claim support for an unrealized object. 
Theorem 3.14.8.2 (Faithfulness Requirement) 
The theorem uses established semantics-preservation reasoning. The framework-specific condition is that preservation is evaluated relative to Compatibility–ICG architectural invariants rather than surface equality of program values.  A computational operation fᶜ faithfully realizes an architectural operation fᴬ on domain D when 
ρᶜ(fᴬ(a)) = fᶜ(ρᶜ(a))  for every a ∈ D
and every required architectural invariant is preserved. 
Proof 
The equality states that applying the mathematical operation and then realizing its result agrees with realizing the input and applying the computational operation. Invariant preservation prevents a numerically equal output from being accepted when its architectural type, provenance, admissibility, or realization status is incorrect. These conditions are necessary and sufficient for faithfulness on D by definition. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This is not a claim that code proves the mathematics. It states the correspondence obligation that code must satisfy after the mathematical operation has been defined.

3.14.8.4 Foundational Typed Representation 
Dataclasses, enumerations, generics, immutable identifiers, and protocol interfaces are established software-engineering mechanisms. The distinctive contribution here is the type discipline imposed by the architecture: observations, estimates, assumptions, states, constraints, and decisions may not be silently interchanged. 
from __future__ import annotations from dataclasses import dataclass, field from enum import Enum from typing import Callable, Generic, Iterable, Mapping, Protocol, Sequence, TypeVar  T = TypeVar("T")  class EvidenceStatus(Enum):     OBSERVED = "observed"     ESTIMATED = "estimated"     ASSUMED = "assumed"  @dataclass(frozen=True) class ProvenanceRecord:     source_id: str     method: str     timestamp: str     status: EvidenceStatus  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Estimate(Generic[T]):     value: T     lower: T | None     upper: T | None     unit: str     provenance: tuple[ProvenanceRecord, ...]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class ParticipantId:     value: str  @dataclass(frozen=True) class StateId:     value: str  @dataclass(frozen=True) class BoundaryId:     value: str  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Observation(Generic[T]):     subject: str     construct: str     value: T     unit: str     provenance: ProvenanceRecord 
The EvidenceStatus enumeration prevents an assumed compatibility value from being displayed as though it were observed. Estimate carries interval, unit, and provenance fields so that scalar output cannot silently erase uncertainty or source history. 
3.14.8.5 Architectural Objects 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class CompatibilityRelation:     source: ParticipantId     target: ParticipantId     estimate: Estimate[float]     context: str  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Constraint:     name: str     predicate: Callable[["State"], bool]     provenance: tuple[ProvenanceRecord, ...]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class ConstraintArchitecture:     constraints: tuple[Constraint, ...]      def admits(self, state: "State") -> bool:         return all(c.predicate(state) for c in self.constraints)  @dataclass(frozen=True) class State:     id: StateId     attributes: Mapping[str, float]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Boundary:     id: BoundaryId     separating_regions: tuple[str, str]     generators: tuple[str, ...]     uncertainty: Estimate[float]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Selector:     name: str     parent: str | None     unrealized_compatibility: Estimate[float]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Pathway:     name: str     objective: str     selector: str     transitions: tuple[tuple[StateId, StateId], ...]  @dataclass(frozen=True) class Trajectory:     name: str     objective: str     states: tuple[StateId, ...]     pathway: Pathway 
Theorem 3.14.8.3 (Type-Separation Safety Theorem) 
If the implementation requires Observation, Estimate, Constraint, State, Boundary, Pathway, and Trajectory to be distinct types and all transformation functions declare their input and output types, then a type-valid implementation cannot silently substitute one architectural category for another. 
Proof 
A type-valid call accepts only values belonging to its declared domain. Since the listed categories are distinct and possess no implicit coercions, substitution requires an explicit translation function. The translation is therefore inspectable and can be validated against its architectural definition. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
Type safety does not prove construct validity. It prevents one important computational error: treating a convenient numerical representation as though it were the architectural object itself. 
3.14.8.6 Input Contract for the Continuing Organizational Example 
The organizational example contains Engineering, Operations, and Leadership, but no measured compatibility values were supplied. The implementation therefore accepts records rather than embedding invented numbers. 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class OrganizationalInput:     participants: tuple[ParticipantId, ...]     observations: tuple[Observation[float], ...]     compatibility: tuple[CompatibilityRelation, ...]     architecture: ConstraintArchitecture     states: tuple[State, ...]     boundaries: tuple[Boundary, ...]     selectors: tuple[Selector, ...]  engineering = ParticipantId("Engineering") operations = ParticipantId("Operations") leadership = ParticipantId("Leadership")  # Measurements are supplied by an empirical study. # No numerical compatibility, pressure, legitimacy, or energy values # are invented in this demonstration. 
This is a valid computational instantiation of the participant types without pretending to instantiate unmeasured quantities. A future data adapter may load validated records from a database, file, survey, event log, or causal-estimation pipeline while preserving the same contract. 
3.14.8.7 Boundary Reconstruction Interface 
Boundary detection is not equivalent to selecting every negative edge. A boundary is inferred from a declared classification or transition model, its defining constraints, and uncertainty. The interface therefore separates estimation from thresholding. 
class BoundaryEstimator(Protocol):     def fit(         self,         observations: Sequence[Observation[float]],         architecture: ConstraintArchitecture,     ) -> tuple[Boundary, ...]: ...  @dataclass(frozen=True) class ReconstructionFamily:     architectures: tuple[ConstraintArchitecture, ...]     boundaries: tuple[tuple[Boundary, ...], ...]     assumptions: tuple[str, ...]   def reconstruct_candidates(     observations: Sequence[Observation[float]],     hypotheses: Sequence[ConstraintArchitecture],     estimator: BoundaryEstimator, ) -> ReconstructionFamily:     surviving_architectures = []     surviving_boundaries = []     for architecture in hypotheses:         boundaries = estimator.fit(observations, architecture)         if observations_are_compatible(observations, architecture, boundaries):             surviving_architectures.append(architecture)             surviving_boundaries.append(boundaries)     return ReconstructionFamily(         tuple(surviving_architectures),         tuple(surviving_boundaries),         assumptions=("Candidate family is model-class relative.",),     ) 
The undefined function observations_are_compatible is an intentionally explicit extension point. Its statistical test, tolerance, and error model must be defined by the empirical deployment. The function returns a family rather than a unique architecture, preserving reconstruction non-injectivity. 
3.14.8.8 Projection Interfaces 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class ProjectionBundle:     compatibility: object     recovery: object     diversity: object     resonance: object     pressure: object     representation: object     legitimacy: object     reachability: object     amplitude: object     energy: object   def construct_projections(     system: OrganizationalInput,     estimators: Mapping[str, Callable[[OrganizationalInput], object]], ) -> ProjectionBundle:     required = {         "compatibility", "recovery", "diversity", "resonance",         "pressure", "representation", "legitimacy", "reachability",         "amplitude", "energy",     }     missing = required.difference(estimators)     if missing:         raise ValueError(f"Missing projection estimators: {sorted(missing)}")     return ProjectionBundle(**{name: estimators[name](system) for name in required}) 
The generic object return type marks the section boundary between architecture and estimator-specific implementations. Section 3.14.7 specifies what every estimator must report. A production implementation should replace object with concrete validated result types. 
3.14.8.9 Recovery and Selector Redeployment 
def nearest_recoverable_ancestor(     failed_selector: Selector,     selectors: Mapping[str, Selector],     threshold: float, ) -> Selector | None:     current: Selector | None = failed_selector     visited: set[str] = set()     while current is not None:         if current.name in visited:             raise ValueError("Selector ancestry contains a cycle")         visited.add(current.name)         if current.unrealized_compatibility.lower is None:             raise ValueError("Uᴿ lower bound is required")         if current.unrealized_compatibility.lower > threshold:             return current         current = selectors.get(current.parent) if current.parent else None     return None   def redeploy_pathway(     failed_pathway: Pathway,     alternative: Pathway,     ancestor: Selector, ) -> Pathway:     if alternative.objective != failed_pathway.objective:         raise ValueError("Objective preservation failed")     if alternative.selector != ancestor.name:         raise ValueError("Alternative was not deployed by the recovery selector")     return alternative 
The function uses the lower uncertainty bound of Uᴿ rather than the point estimate, preventing unsupported recovery classification. It also detects cyclic ancestry and enforces objective preservation. The pathway may fail without invalidating the objective; redeployment occurs only through an ancestral selector with certified unrealized compatibility. 
Theorem 3.14.8.4 (Computational Pathway-Recovery Correspondence) 
Assume the selector mapping represents the mathematical ancestry relation, the lower bound in each Uᴿ estimate is valid at the declared confidence or credibility level, and the ancestry is finite and acyclic. Then nearest_recoverable_ancestor returns the nearest ancestor whose certified Uᴿ exceeds the threshold, or None if no such ancestor exists. 
Proof 
The algorithm begins at the failed selector and traverses one parent at a time. It returns at the first satisfying selector. Every previously visited selector is strictly closer and failed the condition. Finite acyclicity guarantees termination. If traversal reaches no satisfying selector, None is returned. Thus the result agrees with the nearest-ancestor rule. 
∎ 
3.14.8.10 Reachability and Recovery Corridors 
def reachable_states(     initial: StateId,     states: Mapping[StateId, State],     transitions: Mapping[StateId, Sequence[StateId]],     architecture: ConstraintArchitecture, ) -> frozenset[StateId]:     visited: set[StateId] = set()     frontier = [initial]     while frontier:         current = frontier.pop()         if current in visited:             continue         state = states[current]         if not architecture.admits(state):             continue         visited.add(current)         frontier.extend(transitions.get(current, ()))     return frozenset(visited) 
This finite-state breadth/depth search realizes Reach(x;Γ) only for the supplied discrete transition relation. Continuous systems require a separately justified reachability method and error bound. Changing Γ and recomputing the set realizes intervention as a transformation of the reachable-future landscape. 
3.14.8.11 Pressure, Representation, and Legitimacy Contracts 
class PressureEstimator(Protocol):     def estimate(self, state: State, boundary: Boundary) -> Estimate[float]: ...  class RepresentationEstimator(Protocol):     def estimate(self, participant: ParticipantId, boundary: Boundary) -> Estimate[float]: ...  class LegitimacyEstimator(Protocol):     def estimate(         self,         boundary: Boundary,         affected: Sequence[ParticipantId],     ) -> Estimate[float]: ...   def pressure_asymmetry(a: Estimate[float], b: Estimate[float]) -> Estimate[float]:     if a.unit != b.unit:         raise ValueError("Pressure units are not comparable")     value = abs(a.value - b.value)     lower = None if a.lower is None or b.upper is None else max(0.0, a.lower - b.upper, b.lower - a.upper)     upper = None if a.upper is None or b.lower is None else max(abs(a.upper - b.lower), abs(b.upper - a.lower))     return Estimate(value, lower, upper, a.unit, a.provenance + b.provenance) 
The estimator protocols prevent a philosophical interpretation of coercion or legitimacy from being mistaken for a measured scalar. A deployment must define the observation model, scale, invariance tests, and uncertainty procedure before these interfaces can be implemented. 
3.14.8.12 Amplitude, Energy, and Resonance Contracts 
class AmplitudeEstimator(Protocol):     def estimate(self, locus: str) -> Estimate[float]: ...  class EnergyFunctional(Protocol):     def state_energy(self, state: State) -> Estimate[float]: ...     def trajectory_energy(self, trajectory: Trajectory) -> Estimate[float]: ...  @dataclass(frozen=True) class ResonanceMode:     eigenvalue: Estimate[float]     support: tuple[str, ...]     vector: tuple[float, ...]  class ResonanceEstimator(Protocol):     def modes(self, system: OrganizationalInput) -> tuple[ResonanceMode, ...]: ... 
Numerical eigendecomposition, norms, and energy integration are established computational methods. The framework-specific content is the construction of the operator and functional from compatibility-supported, constraint-admissible organizational relations. A shared slogan is not a resonance mode; support and aligned response must be estimated. 
3.14.8.13 Cross-Projection Consistency 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class ConsistencyResult:     passed: bool     reasons: tuple[str, ...]   def check_joint_consistency(     trajectory: Trajectory,     reachable: frozenset[StateId],     objective_preserved: bool,     structural_recovery: bool,     pressure_ok: bool,     representation_ok: bool,     legitimacy_ok: bool,     resonance_ok: bool,     energy_ok: bool, ) -> ConsistencyResult:     tests = {         "trajectory leaves reachable set": all(s in reachable for s in trajectory.states),         "objective is not preserved": objective_preserved,         "obstruction architecture remains active": structural_recovery,         "pressure condition failed": pressure_ok,         "representation condition failed": representation_ok,         "legitimacy condition failed": legitimacy_ok,         "resonance condition failed": resonance_ok,         "energy condition failed": energy_ok,     }     failures = tuple(reason for reason, passed in tests.items() if not passed)     return ConsistencyResult(not failures, failures) 
The function records why a trajectory is rejected. It does not conceal elimination inside a composite score. This realizes the filtering-by-elimination methodology and preserves an auditable consequence archive. 
3.14.8.14 False-Recovery Test 
def structural_recovery_established(     outcome_improved: bool,     obstruction_changed: bool,     obstruction_bypassed_admissibly: bool,     residual_upper_bound: float | None,     residual_tolerance: float, ) -> bool:     if not outcome_improved:         return False     architecture_repaired = obstruction_changed or obstruction_bypassed_admissibly     residual_controlled = (         residual_upper_bound is not None         and residual_upper_bound <= residual_tolerance     )     return architecture_repaired and residual_controlled 
Outcome improvement is necessary in this implementation but insufficient. Structural recovery additionally requires an admissible change or bypass of the obstruction and uncertainty-qualified residual control. The criterion is configurable because domains may define recovery differently, but the configuration must be declared before evaluation. 
3.14.8.15 Candidate Trajectories from the Worked Example 
The candidates retain the qualitative interventions introduced in Section 3.14.6. No unmeasured scores are assigned. 
candidate_a = "communication-tool replacement" candidate_b = "additional coordination meetings" candidate_c = "shared boundary governance" candidate_d = "objective-preserving selector redeployment"  # Each candidate must be translated into actual State and Trajectory # objects by a validated domain model before evaluation. 
Candidate A may improve latency while preserving the obstruction architecture. Candidate B may increase communication volume while increasing pressure. Candidate C changes participation in boundary generation. Candidate D preserves the objective while redeploying a failed selector pathway. These are hypotheses to be tested, not coded conclusions. 
3.14.8.16 Admissibility Filtering and Nondominance 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class EvaluationVector:     feasibility: float     energy: float     barrier: float     residual: float     pressure_asymmetry: float     legitimacy: float     domination_risk: float     reachable_future_volume: float     resonance_potential: float   def pareto_dominates(a: EvaluationVector, b: EvaluationVector) -> bool:     # Orientation is explicit: higher is preferred for feasibility,     # legitimacy, future volume, and resonance; lower for the rest.     a_values = (         a.feasibility, -a.energy, -a.barrier, -a.residual,         -a.pressure_asymmetry, a.legitimacy, -a.domination_risk,         a.reachable_future_volume, a.resonance_potential,     )     b_values = (         b.feasibility, -b.energy, -b.barrier, -b.residual,         -b.pressure_asymmetry, b.legitimacy, -b.domination_risk,         b.reachable_future_volume, b.resonance_potential,     )     return all(x >= y for x, y in zip(a_values, b_values)) and any(         x > y for x, y in zip(a_values, b_values)     )   def nondominated(     evaluations: Mapping[str, EvaluationVector], ) -> frozenset[str]:     return frozenset(         name for name, vector in evaluations.items()         if not any(             other != name and pareto_dominates(other_vector, vector)             for other, other_vector in evaluations.items()         )     ) 
Pareto comparison is established. The implementation explicitly orients every criterion, avoiding the hidden assumption that every large number is desirable. It returns a surviving landscape, not a unique winner. Uncertainty-aware dominance should replace point dominance in empirical use. 
3.14.8.17 End-to-End Computational Specification 
@dataclass(frozen=True) class ICGReport:     reconstruction: ReconstructionFamily     accepted: tuple[str, ...]     rejected: Mapping[str, tuple[str, ...]]     nondominated: frozenset[str]     assumptions: tuple[str, ...]   def analyze(     system: OrganizationalInput,     hypotheses: Sequence[ConstraintArchitecture],     boundary_estimator: BoundaryEstimator,     candidate_trajectories: Mapping[str, Trajectory],     evaluate: Callable[[Trajectory], tuple[ConsistencyResult, EvaluationVector]], ) -> ICGReport:     reconstruction = reconstruct_candidates(         system.observations, hypotheses, boundary_estimator     )     accepted: dict[str, EvaluationVector] = {}     rejected: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = {}     for name, trajectory in candidate_trajectories.items():         consistency, vector = evaluate(trajectory)         if consistency.passed:             accepted[name] = vector         else:             rejected[name] = consistency.reasons     return ICGReport(         reconstruction=reconstruction,         accepted=tuple(accepted),         rejected=rejected,         nondominated=nondominated(accepted),         assumptions=reconstruction.assumptions,     ) 
The orchestration function performs reconstruction, candidate evaluation, rejection with reasons, and nondominance filtering. It delegates measurement and domain validity to injected estimators, thereby preserving realization-mechanism neutrality and preventing the demonstration from disguising unspecified estimators as completed mathematics. 
Theorem 3.14.8.5 (End-to-End Traceability Theorem) 
Assume every estimator returns provenance-preserving results, every evaluation predicate is linked to a declared architectural condition, and analyze receives finite candidate sets. Then every accepted, rejected, and nondominated trajectory in ICGReport is traceable to supplied observations, assumptions, estimators, and decision rules. 
Proof 
Reconstruction stores assumptions and is generated from supplied observations and hypotheses. Evaluation assigns every rejection an explicit reason. Accepted trajectories retain evaluation vectors used by the deterministic dominance relation. Provenance is carried by every Estimate used by the estimators. Finite iteration terminates. Therefore each output possesses a finite derivation path. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
Traceability establishes auditability, not empirical correctness. Validation, calibration, and causal identification remain mandatory. 
3.14.8.18 Computational Walkthrough Without Fabricated Execution 
A developer or empirical analyst would instantiate the demonstration in the following order: 
Load consented, provenance-preserved observations for the three divisions. 
Operationalize compatibility, constraints, state variables, representation, legitimacy, pressure, amplitude, energy, and resonance. 
Construct a candidate model class and reconstruct the surviving architecture family. 
Estimate boundaries and projection quantities with uncertainty. 
Construct candidate pathways A–D as state sequences under specified selectors. 
Compute reachable sets for each intervention-specific constraint architecture. 
Test objective preservation, structural recovery, pressure, representation, legitimacy, energy, and resonance. 
Reject inadmissible trajectories with reasons. 
Propagate uncertainty into evaluation vectors. 
Return the uncertainty-qualified nondominated intervention landscape. 
Validate predictions prospectively before authorizing action. 
No printed output is supplied because the treatise contains no empirical records from which such output could be justified. The absence of invented output is part of the rigor of the demonstration, not an incompleteness in the code architecture. 
3.14.8.19 Realization–Architecture Correspondence Theorem 
The theorem below uses established implementation-refinement reasoning. The contribution specific to the treatise is the explicit correspondence among Compatibility, ICG, recovery, resonance, pressure, representation, legitimacy, and reachability objects within one software realization. 
For every implemented object in this section, there exists a previously defined mathematical object to which it is assigned by ρᶜ. For every implemented operation claimed to realize an architectural operation, the faithfulness obligation of Theorem 3.14.8.2 applies. 
Proof 
ParticipantId, State, ConstraintArchitecture, Boundary, Selector, Pathway, Trajectory, Estimate, and ProjectionBundle are assigned to their corresponding mathematical types. Reconstruction, ancestry search, reachability, consistency filtering, false-recovery testing, and Pareto filtering are assigned to previously defined architectural operations. The implementation is therefore a computational realization precisely on the subdomain where the correspondence and invariants have been verified. No claim is made for unspecified estimators or unverified extensions. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The code is neither a metaphor nor an independent source of truth. It is a reviewable realization contract whose adequacy can be tested against the mathematics. 
3.14.8.20 Provenance, Contribution, and Dependency Characterization 
Established mathematics and computation used here include typed data models, graph and state-space representations, reachability search, eigenvalue computation interfaces, uncertainty intervals, feasible-set intersection, Pareto dominance, dependency injection, protocol interfaces, termination on finite sets, and traceable software design. These elements are not introduced by this treatise. 
The new application consists in realizing compatibility, recovery, resonance, pressure, representation, legitimacy, and reachable-future analysis through a shared typed computational architecture. The framework-specific structure is the enforced correspondence among these projections, the separation of objective from pathway and selector, ancestor recovery under certified Uᴿ > 0, boundary-invariance testing for structural recovery, architectural cross-projection filtering, and preservation of realization-mechanism neutrality through injected estimators. 
The implementation depends on the definitions and theorem families of Sections 3.10–3.14.7. It does not replace them. In particular, no function can repair an undefined construct, a non-identifiable quantity, invalid data, or an unjustified causal assumption. 
3.14.8.21 Limitations and Claim Boundary 
The code has not been empirically calibrated against an organizational dataset. 
No numeric compatibility, boundary, pressure, legitimacy, energy, amplitude, resonance, or reachability values are supplied. 
Several estimator interfaces are intentionally unimplemented because their valid realization is domain- and data-dependent. 
Finite-state reachability does not establish reachability for continuous systems. 
Point-valued Pareto filtering is illustrative; empirical deployment must propagate uncertainty. 
A valid Python program can still encode an invalid scientific model. 
No recommendation produced by the implementation carries autonomous authority. 
Accordingly, this section establishes computational realizability and a faithful implementation skeleton. It does not establish empirical success, predictive superiority, causal validity, or deployment readiness. 
3.14.8.22 Concluding Consequence 
The sequence developed across the four sections is now complete at the specification level: 
3.14.5 unification → 3.14.6 comparison → 3.14.7 measurement and computation → 3.14.8 computational realization
The organizational example can be represented by typed observations, reconstructed as an equivalence-qualified architecture, decomposed through multiple ICG projections, searched for recovery ancestry and reachable futures, filtered through cross-projection admissibility, tested for false recovery, and compared through a nondominated intervention landscape. Each operation remains conditional on declared measurements, assumptions, estimators, and validation results. 
The principal achievement of this section is therefore not that code has been written. It is that the mathematical architecture has been translated into a computational contract without collapsing architecture into realization, assumptions into observations, point estimates into certainty, pathway failure into objective failure, or filtering into unjustified winner selection. 
Transition to Section 3.14.9 
The next step is empirical rather than syntactic. A measured demonstration must implement the estimator interfaces, calibrate the constructs, quantify uncertainty, compare against strong baselines, test predictions prospectively, and evaluate whether the integrated geometry changes real decisions or outcomes. Section 3.14.9 may therefore develop an Empirical Demonstration and Validation Protocol for ICG. 
3.14.9 Historical Validation Demonstration: Nokia, 2007–2013 
3.14.9.1 Objective and Claim Boundary 
Sections 3.14.5–3.14.8 established the unification, comparative, measurement, computational, and realization architectures of Interoperability Constraint Geometry. The present section asks a narrower historical question: when the architecture is restricted to contemporaneous public evidence from 2007, does it generate explicit structural expectations that are consistent with Nokia’s subsequently documented 2013 outcome? 
This is a historical validation demonstration, not a prospective trial. The 2013 outcome is already known to the present author and reader; therefore the procedure cannot eliminate all analyst hindsight. Its rigor instead rests on a frozen evidence boundary, claim-level provenance, explicit separation of observation from inference, and pre-reveal predictions stated using only the admitted 2007 record. The result may establish historical consistency and diagnostic usefulness. It cannot by itself establish universal validity, causal identification, calibrated predictive accuracy, or superiority over every classical method. 
Provenance is integrated throughout. The financial, organizational, and risk statements are established source evidence. Their use as classical strategy inputs is an application of established analytical practice. Compatibility pressure, boundary geometry, unrealized compatibility, resonance support, and reachability are framework-specific reconstructions introduced by ICG. 
3.14.9.2 Validation Methodology and Information Firewall 
Definition 3.14.9.1 (Frozen Evidence Set) 
E₂₀₀₇ = {CR-01,…,CR-12, AR-01,…,AR-08}.
The set contains only statements extracted from Nokia’s 2007 Corporate Responsibility Report and Nokia in 2007. Each statement is identified by source, printed page, and PDF page. The 2013 reports are quarantined until Section 3.14.9.8. 
Definition 3.14.9.2 (Admissible Historical Prediction) 
P is admissible ⇔ P = f(E₂₀₀₇, C(E₂₀₀₇), I(E₂₀₀₇)) and ∂P/∂O₂₀₁₃ = 0.
Here C is a declared classical inference map, I is the declared ICG reconstruction map, and O₂₀₁₃ denotes outcome evidence. The derivative notation is structural: no inferential dependency on the quarantined outcome is permitted. 
Definition 3.14.9.3 (Validation Relation) 
Val(P,O) ∈ {supported, contradicted, unresolved}.
A prediction is supported when the later primary-source outcome contains the predicted structural event; contradicted when the outcome contains an incompatible event; and unresolved when the outcome sources do not discriminate the prediction. “Supported” is not synonymous with “caused by,” “uniquely predicted by,” or “proved universally.” 
Theorem 3.14.9.1 (Historical Integrity Theorem) 
If every premise of P is traceable to E₂₀₀₇ and every transformation is declared before O₂₀₁₃ is consulted, then P is evidentially independent of O₂₀₁₃ within the documented derivation. 
Proof 
By construction, the dependency graph of P has leaves only in E₂₀₀₇ and internal nodes only in declared classical or ICG transformations. O₂₀₁₃ is absent from that graph. Therefore no formal dependency on O₂₀₁₃ exists in the documented derivation. This does not erase analyst prior knowledge; it establishes an auditable information firewall in the written argument. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem protects derivational integrity while expressly declining the stronger claim of a prospective blind forecast.

Within the frozen 2007 evidence, substantial financial and innovation resources do not suffice to establish compatibility of Nokia’s transformation pathway.

3.14.9.7 Visible Walkthrough Before Outcome Reveal 
Step 1 — Visible success. Net sales rose 24% to EUR 51 058 million. A dashboard centered on current realized output is green. 
Step 2 — Visible adaptive capacity. R&D expense was EUR 5 647 million; Nokia established research and innovation centers, created services, and pursued mapping capability. Resource availability is also green. 
Step 3 — Visible boundary load. Nokia simultaneously reorganized, integrated Nokia Siemens Networks, expanded devices and services, and moved toward converging internet and communications industries. The architecture is not static. 
Step 4 — Explicit risk condition. Nokia itself stated that failure to maintain a competitive portfolio could materially harm business, market share, and operating results, while competition was intense. 
Step 5 — ICG separation. The first two steps establish capability and positive unrealized compatibility. They do not establish that the current selector and pathway can combine those capabilities quickly enough. The reader therefore sees hidden recoverability and pathway risk at the same time: Uᴿ > 0, yet pathway compatibility remains unresolved. 
Step 6 — Frozen expectation. If the device pathway fails, the architecture predicts neither total objective failure nor total organizational disappearance. It predicts pathway contraction plus possible redeployment into surviving capability regions.

3.14.9.10 Comparative Validation Analysis 
The classical reconstruction correctly identifies dominance, investment, transformation, competition, and conditional strategy risk. ICG does not earn credit merely for restating those facts. Its incremental contribution is the structure of the conditional claim: resources and objectives are separated from selectors and pathways; present performance is separated from future reachability; local pathway failure is separated from total objective failure; and recovery is represented as redeployment through surviving compatibility rather than restoration of the failed realization. 
Observed strength ≠ pathway compatibility.
Pathway failure ≠ objective failure.
Residual capability + selector redeployment ⇒ architectural survival may coexist with local collapse.
Theorem 3.14.9.4 (Nokia Historical Consistency Theorem) 
For the frozen source set used here, the 2013 Nokia outcome is consistent with the ICG prediction family P-01 through P-05, and no listed prediction is contradicted by the admitted outcome evidence. 
Proof 
P-01 anticipates deterioration of an affected pathway despite strong initial performance; O-01–O-03 establish sale and discontinuation of Devices & Services. P-02 anticipates residual capability; O-05 establishes continuing capability regions. P-03 and P-04 anticipate selector redeployment and architectural contraction rather than total disappearance; O-01–O-05 establish reconfiguration around remaining businesses. P-05 anticipates that current strength is not sufficient; AR-01 and O-01–O-03 jointly exhibit that separation across the historical interval. Therefore the outcome supports the listed qualitative predictions at the resolution of the available evidence. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem establishes historical consistency, not exclusive explanatory ownership. Classical strategy analysis could also anticipate risk. The ICG gain is the unified relation among strength, obstruction, unrealized compatibility, pathway failure, redeployment, and survival. 
Theorem 3.14.9.5 (Hidden Recoverability Demonstration Theorem) 
The Nokia case visibly demonstrates hidden recoverability in the restricted sense that positive unrealized compatibility in 2007 is followed by survival of capability regions despite failure and disposal of a major realization pathway. 
Proof 
CR-07, CR-09, AR-02, AR-05, and AR-06 establish service, research, software, and mapping resources beyond a single static handset pathway. O-01–O-05 establish disposal of Devices & Services while continuing businesses remained. Thus the objective space did not collapse with the failed pathway. This is precisely the pathway-recovery distinction: surviving compatibility can support redeployment even when return along the original path is unavailable. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The demonstration does not claim that ICG caused Nokia’s recovery or that every hidden resource was realized. It shows that the architecture’s separation of objective, selector, pathway, and residual capability matches the observed historical form. 
3.14.9.11 Falsification and Unresolved Questions 
The case would contradict the pathway/objective distinction if disposal of Devices & Services necessarily eliminated every adjacent capability and objective region; the 2013 evidence does not show that. 
The case does not validate numerical pressure, legitimacy, representation, resonance, or reachability measures because no calibrated 2007 series was available. 
The case does not identify the unique internal organizational cause of the outcome. 
The case does not demonstrate superior forecast accuracy over a preregistered classical benchmark. 
The case cannot eliminate hindsight bias because the reconstruction was performed after the outcome; the evidence firewall mitigates but does not remove that limitation. 
A prospective study must freeze data, model, thresholds, predictions, and benchmark methods before outcomes occur. 
3.14.9.12 Provenance, Novelty, and Dependency Map 
Established mathematics and methods used here include evidence freezing, dependency graphs, ordinal inference, falsification criteria, conditional prediction, and comparative case analysis. The use of contemporaneous corporate reports as historical evidence is standard documentary practice.  The new application is the use of those methods to reconstruct Nokia’s 2007–2013 transition as a controlled historical test of an interoperability geometry. 
The framework-specific contribution is the joint architecture connecting compatibility pressure, boundary load, unrealized compatibility Uᴿ, selector/pathway separation, obstruction horizons, reachability contraction, and recovery by redeployment. The dependency chain is: contemporaneous observations → classical inferences → ICG reconstruction → frozen predictions → quarantined outcome → validation relation.

3.14.9.14 Conclusion and Transition 
The Nokia demonstration makes the architecture visible. In 2007, current performance, investment, and innovation capacity were strong; simultaneously, rapid convergence, reorganization, portfolio dependence, and intense competition made pathway compatibility decisive. ICG does not reinterpret strength as weakness. It shows why strength and obstruction can coexist. The 2013 outcome then exhibits the predicted form: a major pathway was disposed of, the broader organization survived, and residual capability supported architectural redeployment. 
The next section must convert this retrospective historical consistency test into a prospective validation architecture. Section 3.14.10 should therefore specify preregistration, measurement intervals, benchmark models, calibrated ICG quantities, blinded outcome windows, error metrics, confidence procedures, and conditions under which the framework must be rejected or revised. 
3.14.10 Prospective Validation and Falsification Architecture 
3.14.10.1 Objective and Architectural Position 
Section 3.14.9 established a controlled historical consistency demonstration. Contemporaneous Nokia evidence was frozen, classical and ICG reconstructions were separated, qualitative predictions were stated before the outcome reveal, and later primary-source observations were used to evaluate those predictions. That demonstration established that the ICG pathway–recovery architecture was consistent with a documented historical transition. It did not establish prospective predictive validity, calibrated accuracy, causal identification, or superiority over benchmark methods. 
The present section constructs the architecture required to test such stronger claims. Its governing transition is: 
historical explanation  →  preregistered prediction  →  withheld outcome  →  falsification  →  revision.
The objective is not to protect ICG from failure. The objective is to make failure observable, attributable, and scientifically productive. A framework that can reinterpret every outcome after it occurs is architecturally closed against correction. A prospectively accountable framework must instead preserve an admissible path from adverse evidence to model revision, local theorem restriction, measurement correction, or rejection of the relevant prediction family. 
Established methods used here include preregistration, temporal holdout, benchmark comparison, proper scoring, calibration, confidence procedures, survival analysis, reliability assessment, and falsification. Their use in organizational and relational systems is an application of existing empirical methodology. The framework-specific contribution is the registry and validation architecture that connects those methods to compatibility boundaries, pressure, resonance, legitimacy, representation, recovery, reachability, obstruction horizons, and pathway redeployment.

Validation must attach to a claim class. No single experiment can validate an entire architecture at once.

Definition 3.14.10.1 (Claim–Evidence Admissibility) 
Adm(C,E,M) = 1
if and only if evidence E and method M are sufficient for the logical strength of claim C. Predictive evidence is not automatically causal evidence; historical consistency is not prospective prediction; and accurate classification is not calibrated probability estimation. 
Theorem 3.14.10.1 (Claim-Strength Monotonicity Theorem) 
If claim C₂ logically entails claim C₁ but C₁ does not entail C₂, then evidence sufficient only for C₁ is insufficient for C₂. 
Proof 
Assume E is sufficient for C₁ but contains no information resolving the additional proposition required by C₂. Since C₂ entails C₁ plus at least one further condition, E leaves that condition undecided. Therefore E cannot warrant C₂. Applied here, historical consistency may support reconstructive plausibility but cannot alone warrant prospective or causal validity. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem uses elementary logical implication. Its distinctive application is to prevent the ICG program from moving silently among descriptive, predictive, comparative, causal, and design claims. 
3.14.10.3 Prospective Validation Task 
Definition 3.14.10.2 (Prospective Validation Task) 
𝒱 = (O₀, 𝒟, Mᴮ, Mᴵ, P, F, W, O₁, S).
Here O₀ is the information available at registration time t₀; 𝒟 is the declared data-generating and measurement protocol; Mᴮ is the locked benchmark model family; Mᴵ is the locked ICG model family; P is the prediction register; F is the falsifier register; W = [t₀,t₁] is the outcome window; O₁ is the outcome record revealed after t₁; and S is the scoring rule fixed before outcome access. 
Definition 3.14.10.3 (Temporal Information Firewall) 
σ(O₀,𝒟,Mᴮ,Mᴵ,P,F,S)  ∩  σ(O₁) = ∅  before t₁,
where σ(·) denotes the information generated by its arguments. Operationally, the model-development team must not access outcome information from the withheld interval, directly or through proxy leakage. 
Theorem 3.14.10.2 (Prospective Integrity Theorem) 
If the temporal information firewall holds, all preprocessing and models are locked before t₁, and outcome adjudication follows the registered protocol, then the documented prediction is prospectively independent of the withheld outcome. 
Proof 
The derivation graph of P contains only O₀, the declared measurement process, and locked transformations. O₁ is generated or disclosed only after the graph is frozen. Therefore no formal edge from O₁ to P exists. Hidden leakage, protocol deviation, or undocumented analyst intervention violates a premise and must be reported. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
Unlike the historical integrity result, this theorem can support a genuinely prospective claim, provided implementation audit confirms its premises.

Theorem 3.14.10.3 (Prediction Traceability Theorem) 
Every valid registered prediction has a finite, inspectable dependency path from source observation to evaluated claim.

∎ 
Interpretation 
Traceability does not prove correctness; it localizes error and makes correction possible. 
3.14.10.5 Falsification and Revision Architecture 
Definition 3.14.10.5 (Strong Falsifier) 
For prediction P with admissible outcome space Ω, a strong falsifier is a nonempty set F ⊂ Ω such that observing O₁ ∈ F contradicts P under the registered assumptions. 
Definition 3.14.10.6 (Weak Falsifier) 
A weak falsifier is an observation that materially decreases support for P but does not logically contradict it because nuisance parameters, measurement error, or unresolved identifiability remain. 
Definition 3.14.10.7 (Revision Locality) 
When a prediction fails, revision must first target the nearest invalid dependency: measurement, observation, inference, reconstruction, model, or theorem scope. Failure shall not automatically be propagated to the entire objective or framework. 
failure(P)  ⇒  inspect nearest invalid ancestor, not reject all descendants indiscriminately. 
Theorem 3.14.10.4 (Prospective Falsifiability Theorem) 
A predictive ICG claim has empirical discriminative content only if its falsifier set has positive admissible measure or positive registered probability under at least one competing data-generating process. 
Proof 
If F is empty or impossible under every admissible process, no possible observation can distinguish P from its negation. P then imposes no empirical restriction on Ω. Conversely, a nonempty reachable F makes at least one observation incompatible with P and permits discrimination. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This adapts established falsifiability reasoning to geometric claims. Statements such as “pressure mattered somehow” are inadmissible; a registered increase, threshold crossing, ordering, or event window must expose the claim to failure. 
Theorem 3.14.10.5 (Local Failure Theorem) 
Failure of a registered prediction invalidates at least one dependency on its derivation path but does not, without further proof, invalidate unrelated ICG structures. 
Proof 
A prediction is a composition of observation, measurement, assumptions, reconstruction, and forecast map. If the output fails, at least one component or composition relation is inadequate. Components outside the dependency graph are not logically implicated. Therefore failure localizes before it globalizes. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This is the validation analogue of pathway failure rather than objective failure. 
3.14.10.6 Measurement Schedule and Blinded Outcome Windows 
Definition 3.14.10.8 (Measurement Schedule) 
𝒯 = {t₋k,…,t₀,t₁,…,tₘ}.
The pre-registration times estimate baseline geometry; t₀ freezes the prediction; t₁,…,tₘ constitute blinded monitoring and outcome windows. Sampling frequency must be justified by the expected temporal scale of transitions, not selected after observing the event. 
Definition 3.14.10.9 (Embargoed Outcome Window) 
Wᵉ = (t₀,t₁],
during which outcome labels, adjudications, and downstream proxies are withheld from model revision. Safety-critical monitoring may continue, but any intervention or unblinding must be documented and the affected validation classified accordingly. 
Missingness, censoring, participant attrition, regime change, and intervention contamination must be registered. When the system changes so substantially that the original measurement invariance no longer holds, the correct classification is unresolved or transport failure—not an automatic predictive success or failure. 
3.14.10.7 Benchmark and Ablation Architecture 
ICG must be compared with the strongest reasonable benchmark portfolio receiving identical information. Candidate baselines include persistence, trend, generalized linear or survival models, network statistics, systems-dynamics indicators, machine-learning forecasts, governance indices, resilience measures, and domain-expert judgment. Selection must occur before outcome reveal. 
Definition 3.14.10.10 (Incremental ICG Contribution) 
Δᴵ = S(Mᴮ,O₁) − S(Mᴵ,O₁)
for loss scores where lower is better. For utility scores the sign is reversed. Positive Δᴵ indicates improvement over the registered benchmark. Confidence intervals or resampling procedures must preserve dependence and clustering in the data. 
Definition 3.14.10.11 (Projection Ablation) 
For projection j, let Mᴵ⁻ʲ be the ICG model with the j-th projection removed. Its marginal contribution is 
Aⱼ = S(Mᴵ⁻ʲ,O₁) − S(Mᴵ,O₁).
Ablations may be defined for recovery, pressure, representation, legitimacy, resonance, boundary, and reachability projections. A nonpositive Aⱼ does not prove the projection mathematically meaningless; it shows no incremental predictive contribution in the tested task at the tested resolution. 
Theorem 3.14.10.6 (Comparative Information Gain Theorem) 
If Mᴵ and Mᴮ use identical frozen evidence, are evaluated on the same withheld outcomes under the same proper score, and Δᴵ is positive beyond the registered uncertainty criterion, then Mᴵ supplies prospective predictive information not captured by Mᴮ in that task. 
Proof 
Identical inputs remove informational advantage. A proper score rewards truthful predictive distributions. A positive, uncertainty-qualified difference therefore arises from model structure or estimation rather than privileged evidence. The conclusion is task-specific and does not establish universal superiority. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This is the prospective version of the comparative architecture developed in Section 3.14.6. 
3.14.10.8 Calibration, Discrimination, and Error Metrics 
No single metric is sufficient. Discrimination asks whether higher-risk states fail more often; calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. A model may rank correctly while assigning distorted probabilities, or calibrate marginally while failing to discriminate individuals or trajectories. 
Target 
Primary metric family 
Required companion 
Binary failure 
Log loss or Brier score; AUROC/AUPRC. 
Calibration curve; prevalence; confusion costs. 
Time to obstruction 
Time-dependent Brier score; concordance; survival calibration. 
Censoring model and horizon-specific error. 
Reachable-state set 
Precision/recall, Jaccard, coverage of realized states. 
Set-size penalty and unreachable-state audit. 
Trajectory ranking 
Kendall/Spearman rank agreement; regret. 
Decision utility and dominance violations.

Event detection precision/recall and lead time. 
Corridor definition and intervention contamination.

Recurrence prediction, durability survival curve.

Alarm burden and missed-event cost.

Multiclass log score, ranked probability score. 
Classwise calibration and uncertainty. 
Definition 3.14.10.12 (Calibration Error) 
CE = Σᵦ (nᵦ/n) |ȳᵦ − p̄ᵦ|,
where bins b are preregistered, p̄ᵦ is mean predicted probability, and ȳᵦ is observed frequency. Because binned calibration can conceal local error, smooth calibration estimates and uncertainty bands should accompany CE when sample size permits.

3.14.10.9 Hidden Recoverability Protocol 
The claim Uᴿ > 0 concerns surviving compatibility not exhausted by the current realization. It must not be validated merely because some later improvement occurs. 
Definition 3.14.10.14 (Operational Recovery Corridor) 
A registered corridor is a sequence of admissible state transitions γ = (x₀,…,xₙ) satisfying the declared constraints and reaching a recovery state R without violating legitimacy, representation, or safety conditions. 
γ ∈ 𝒯* = 𝒯ᶜ ∩ 𝒯ᴿ ∩ 𝒯ᴾ ∩ 𝒯ᴸ ∩ 𝒯ᴿᵉᵖ ∩ 𝒯ᴿᵉˢ.
A hidden-recoverability test registers: the obstructed pathway; the nearest ancestor with hypothesized Uᴿ > 0; candidate selectors; corridor-defining transitions; incompatible transitions; horizon; and evidence that would show no corridor existed. 
Theorem 3.14.10.7 (Hidden Recoverability Validation Theorem) 
A preregistered hidden-recoverability prediction is supported only if a corridor satisfying the registered admissibility conditions is observed or independently verified within the horizon; mere outcome improvement is insufficient. 
Proof 
Outcome improvement may arise through suppression, external subsidy, domination, measurement drift, or an unregistered mechanism. The target claim concerns an admissible path supported by residual compatibility. Therefore validation requires corridor evidence and satisfaction of the registered constraints, not only a favorable endpoint. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This theorem prevents recovery from being reduced to performance recovery. 
3.14.10.10 False-Recovery Protocol 
Definition 3.14.10.15 (Durable Structural Recovery) 
Recᴰ(t₀,t₁) = Perf↑ ∧ Obstruction↓ ∧ Reach↑ ∧ ND = 1 over Wᴰ, 
where Wᴰ is a preregistered durability window and ND contains the relevant non-domination, legitimacy, and representation constraints. The exact operationalization is domain-specific. 
Definition 3.14.10.16 (False-Recovery Candidate) 
FR = Perf↑ ∧ ¬(Obstruction↓ ∨ Bypassᵃᵈᵐ ∨ ConstraintResolution).
The candidate becomes a validated false recovery only if the apparent improvement fails the durability test or recurrence occurs as predicted. If durable improvement persists despite no detected boundary change, the false-recovery model is weakened and the measurement of obstruction must be reassessed. 
Theorem 3.14.10.8 (False-Recovery Falsifiability Theorem) 
A false-recovery prediction is falsified when durable improvement persists through the registered horizon while the registered obstruction measure remains unchanged and no hidden admissible bypass is detected. 
Proof 
The prediction asserts that unchanged obstruction prevents durable recovery. Persistence of recovery under the stated conditions realizes the strong falsifier. One must then revise either the obstruction reconstruction, the necessity claim, or the measurement model. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This makes false recovery a risky prediction rather than an interpretive label applied after recurrence. 
3.14.10.11 Obstruction-Horizon Protocol 
Definition 3.14.10.17 (Obstruction-Horizon State Vector) 
Hₒ(t) = (Pᶜ(t), Θᴮ(t), Vol(Reach(xₜ)), Res(t), Leg(t), Rep(t), Uᴿ(t)).
Pᶜ is compatibility pressure; Θᴮ is a registered boundary-thickness or transition-reserve measure; Vol(Reach(xₜ)) is an explicitly defined reachable-future measure; Res, Leg, and Rep are resonance, legitimacy, and representation measures; and Uᴿ is unrealized compatibility. No component may be assigned a numerical value without the measurement contracts of Section 3.14.7. 
Definition 3.14.10.18 (Obstruction-Horizon Alarm) 
Aₕ(t) = 1{g(Hₒ(t)) ≥ τₕ},
where g and threshold τₕ are calibrated only on training data and frozen before the outcome window. The event definition, lead-time window, and false-alarm cost must also be fixed. 
Theorem 3.14.10.9 (Early-Warning Validation Theorem) 
An obstruction-horizon model demonstrates prospective early-warning capability only if its locked alarms precede registered events with better score or utility than the locked benchmark at an acceptable false-alarm burden. 
Proof 
Precedence alone is insufficient because frequent alarms can precede events by chance. Benchmark advantage, a fixed event definition, lead-time criterion, and false-alarm accounting jointly establish incremental warning value. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The distinctive ICG claim is not merely that deterioration precedes failure, but that relational geometry supplies useful warning beyond ordinary performance metrics. 
3.14.10.12 Reachability and Trajectory-Ranking Protocol 
Definition 3.14.10.19 (Predicted Reachability Set) 
R̂_H(x₀) = {x : ∃ admissible γ from x₀ to x within horizon H}.
The set is generated by filtering rather than winner selection. Candidate futures are removed when constraints, evidence, or transition rules make them inadmissible. Satisfying futures inhabit the surviving projected structure. 
Definition 3.14.10.20 (Reachability Validation) 
A realized state validates inclusion only weakly; nonrealization does not prove exclusion because many reachable states remain unrealized. Stronger validation therefore requires interventions, natural experiments, exhaustive small-state systems, or verified transition models. False inclusion and false exclusion must be evaluated separately. 
Theorem 3.14.10.10 (Reachability Asymmetry Theorem) 
Observation that x is realized supports x ∈ R̂_H(x₀), but failure to observe x does not by itself support x ∉ R̂_H(x₀). 
Proof 
Reachability is existential: one admissible path suffices. Realization supplies such a path when transition records validate it. Nonrealization may reflect selector choice among many reachable futures rather than impossibility. Therefore positive and negative reachability evidence are asymmetric. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem prevents unchosen futures from being mislabeled impossible. 
3.14.10.13 Representation, Legitimacy, and Ethical Admissibility 
Predictive accuracy cannot legitimate an intervention that excludes affected participants, concentrates unreviewable authority, or removes viable exit. Validation therefore has two non-substitutable dimensions: epistemic validity and admissibility validity. 
Definition 3.14.10.21 (Dual Validation) 
Valid*(M,γ) = Validᴱ(M) ∧ Validᴬ(γ),
where Validᴱ concerns measurement and prediction, while Validᴬ requires registered representation, legitimacy, contestability, privacy, safety, and non-domination conditions. A highly accurate model may be inadmissible for deployment; an ethically admissible process may remain scientifically inaccurate. 
Theorem 3.14.10.11 (Accuracy–Legitimacy Non-Substitution Theorem) 
No increase in predictive accuracy alone proves legitimacy, and no legitimacy property alone proves predictive accuracy. 
Proof 
Accuracy is a relation between predictions and outcomes. Legitimacy concerns the authority, participation, justification, contestability, and exit relations governing action. Neither definition entails the other. Hence they must be measured and evaluated separately before conjunction. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This distinction is an essential extension of validation architecture for pluralist coordination systems. 
3.14.10.14 Uncertainty, Robustness, and Transport 
Every estimate must carry uncertainty appropriate to its source: sampling, measurement, model, structural, and intervention uncertainty. Sensitivity analysis must vary thresholds, graph construction, missing-data assumptions, time windows, and plausible alternative reconstructions. Robustness means conclusions survive a declared perturbation class; it does not mean the model is correct. 
Definition 3.14.10.22 (Transport Domain) 
A validation conclusion transports from environment e₁ to e₂ only under declared invariance conditions concerning measurement, participants, constraints, transition rules, and outcome semantics. 
Transport(e₁→e₂) requires Inv(𝒟, Γ, Π, T, Y).
When invariance fails, the model may remain architecture-relative. CDPI requires testing whether the structural relation persists across realization mechanisms, not assuming that numerical parameters or institutional meanings remain unchanged. 
Theorem 3.14.10.12 (Architecture-Relative Validity Theorem) 
Prospective success in one environment validates the registered architecture only relative to the tested measurement, population, constraints, and realization conditions unless transport invariants are independently established. 
Proof 
The observed score is generated jointly by model and environment. Without invariance, changes in measurement or transition laws can alter the relation. Therefore external validity requires additional evidence. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This preserves architectural truth without converting local success into an unearned universal claim. 
3.14.10.15 Sequential Testing, Multiplicity, and Stopping 
Repeated monitoring can inflate false discoveries. The protocol must register whether evaluation is fixed-horizon, group-sequential, always-valid, or exploratory. Multiple outcomes, horizons, projections, and subgroups require familywise, false-discovery, hierarchical, or multilevel treatment appropriate to the scientific objective. 
Definition 3.14.10.23 (Stopping Rule) 
A stopping rule specifies when data collection or analysis terminates for success, futility, safety, or resource limits. It must be locked before unblinded outcome inspection unless an independent safety mechanism requires intervention. Exploratory analyses remain valuable but must be labeled as hypothesis-generating and entered as new preregistrations rather than retroactively promoted to confirmatory results. 
3.14.10.16 Scientific Admissibility Architecture 
Definition 3.14.10.24 (Scientifically Admissible ICG Study) 
A study is scientifically admissible when it satisfies the following minimum conditions: 
claim class and unit of analysis are declared; 
observations, inferences, reconstructions, and predictions are separated; 
measurement contracts and provenance are fixed; 
benchmark and ICG models receive identical evidence; 
predictions, uncertainty, falsifiers, scores, and horizons are preregistered; 
outcomes are blinded or withheld until the registered time; 
missingness, interventions, protocol deviations, and version changes are logged; 
accuracy and legitimacy are separately evaluated; 
negative, null, unresolved, and contradictory results are publishable; 
revision follows dependency-localized failure analysis. 
Theorem 3.14.10.13 (Scientific Admissibility Theorem) 
If a prospective ICG study satisfies Definition 3.14.10.24 and the registered evaluation is executed without undisclosed deviation, then its result is prospectively testable, auditable, and capable of supporting task-relative scientific revision. 
Proof 
Preregistration prevents outcome-driven specification; the information firewall prevents direct contamination; falsifiers create discriminative content; benchmark parity permits comparison; uncertainty limits strength of inference; provenance and traceability localize error; and publication of adverse outcomes prevents selective survival. Together these conditions make the test accountable to possible failure. They do not guarantee truth, adequate power, or transportability. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
Scientific admissibility is an architecture of accountability, not a certification of correctness.

3.14.10.18 Minimal Prospective Algorithm 
The following algorithm is a realization-neutral protocol. It is not a software implementation and does not privilege any computational mechanism. 
Collect O₀ under a signed measurement contract. 
Construct the classical benchmark from O₀. 
Reconstruct Γ, boundaries, pressure, recovery, reachability, representation, legitimacy, and resonance from O₀. 
Generate candidate predictions and remove any lacking measurable targets or nonempty falsifiers. 
Freeze models, horizons, thresholds, scores, uncertainty procedures, and version hashes. 
Open the embargoed outcome window and prohibit model revision. 
Record interventions and safety-mandated unblinding without concealing them. 
Reveal O₁ after the window closes and apply the locked adjudication. 
Compare benchmark and ICG scores; run registered ablations and sensitivity analyses. 
Classify each claim as supported, contradicted, unresolved, or protocol-invalid. 
Localize failures to the nearest dependency and create new prospective registrations for revisions. 
3.14.10.19 Failure Taxonomy and Recovery Consequences 
Failure class 
Meaning 
Required response 
Measurement failure 
Construct was not measured reliably or invariantly. 
Repair measurement; do not infer architectural failure. 
Reconstruction failure 
Latent geometry is unsupported or nonidentifiable. 
Retain equivalence class, add evidence, or narrow claim.

Registered outcome falls in falsifier set. 
Revise nearest predictive dependency.

Reject incremental-value claim for that task.
