Theorem 3.14.10.14 (Validation Recovery Theorem) 
A failed validation remains scientifically productive when the failure can be localized to a dependency node with a nonempty admissible revision set. 
Proof 
Traceability identifies the nearest failed node. If at least one revision preserves unaffected evidence and constraints while changing the failed component, then unrealized compatibility for the research program remains positive. A new preregistered test can evaluate that revision. If no admissible revision exists, the relevant claim family is retired. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The research program therefore applies its own recovery architecture to itself: obstruction triggers disciplined selector redeployment, not retrospective rescue. 
3.14.10.20 Dependency and Provenance Map 
Established validation methods → measurement contracts → prospective registry → ICG-specific protocols → comparative evaluation → localized revision.
Established mathematics and scientific methods supply probability, scoring, calibration, hypothesis testing, causal identification, survival analysis, graph methods, reliability, and preregistration. Their application here to interoperability geometry is a new recontextualization. The distinctive framework-specific architecture introduced in this section is the integration of those methods with projection-based ICG reconstruction, pathway–objective separation, hidden recoverability, false recovery, obstruction horizons, reachable-future sets, dual epistemic/admissibility validation, and dependency-localized revision. 
The section depends on Section 3.14.4 for boundary geometry, Section 3.14.5 for projection unification, Section 3.14.6 for comparative architecture, Section 3.14.7 for measurement and computation, Section 3.14.8 for realization correspondence, and Section 3.14.9 for the historical evidence firewall. No prospective empirical superiority claim is made here because no registered future study has yet been completed. 
3.14.10.21 Conditions Requiring Rejection or Revision 
The framework must be revised, restricted, or rejected at the appropriate scope when any of the following is established prospectively: 
core ICG measurements cannot achieve acceptable reliability or invariance; 
reconstructions are nonidentifiable in the target domain and the equivalence class is too broad to yield discriminative predictions; 
registered predictions repeatedly fall within their strong falsifier sets; 
ICG adds no predictive or decision value beyond reasonable benchmarks across adequately powered tasks; 
false-recovery, hidden-recoverability, or obstruction-horizon claims cannot be operationalized without circular reference to outcomes; 
reachability predictions systematically omit realized admissible states or include states proven transition-inaccessible; 
legitimacy and representation requirements render proposed deployments inadmissible; 
results depend on undeclared realization mechanisms contrary to CDPI and realization-mechanism neutrality. 
A negative result shall not be reclassified as a success by changing the outcome, horizon, threshold, or claim after unblinding. Any revised claim begins a new prospective lineage. 
3.14.10.22 Concluding Theorem and Transition 
Theorem 3.14.10.15 (Prospective Accountability Theorem) 
The architecture developed in this section converts ICG from a framework capable of historically consistent reconstruction into a research program capable of prospectively accountable prediction, provided its measurement, registration, blinding, benchmark, falsification, scoring, and revision requirements are implemented. 
Proof 
Sections 3.14.10.2–3.14.10.21 define claim classes, validation tasks, information firewalls, typed predictions, falsifiers, measurement windows, benchmarks, metrics, domain-specific tests, admissibility constraints, uncertainty, stopping, registries, algorithms, and failure responses. Their conjunction makes predictions temporally prior to outcomes, empirically restrictive, comparably scored, and revisable under adverse evidence. These are the necessary architectural conditions for prospective accountability. Actual predictive validity remains an empirical question for completed studies. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The result is intentionally conditional. This section earns testability, not success. 
Section 3.14.9 asked whether ICG could reconstruct a known historical transition without collapsing observation into hindsight. The present section asks whether future claims can be exposed to genuine risk. The next section should instantiate this architecture as a Prospective Demonstration Program: select a bounded live system, preregister measurements and benchmarks, freeze ICG predictions and falsifiers, preserve a blinded outcome window, and publish the outcome regardless of direction. 
historical consistency  →  prospective accountability  →  live demonstration  →  cumulative validation.
3.14.11 Prospective Demonstration Program 
3.14.11.1 Objective, Position, and Claim Boundary 
Section 3.14.9 established a retrospectively controlled historical demonstration. Section 3.14.10 then supplied the prospective validation and falsification architecture required to freeze evidence, predictions, falsifiers, benchmarks, outcome windows, scoring rules, admissibility requirements, and revision procedures before outcomes are observed. The present section constructs the program through which those requirements are instantiated repeatedly on live systems. Its purpose is not to announce that Interoperability Constraint Geometry has already achieved prospective validity. Its purpose is to define a mathematically explicit, auditable, and cumulative demonstration program under which such validity may be earned, restricted, revised, or rejected.  The governing transition is therefore 
historical consistency → prospective accountability → registered live demonstration → cumulative evidence → localized revision.
Every demonstration must minimize structural residual Hₜ and maximize validity Vₜ while preserving all admissible evidence, alternatives, falsifiers, and unresolved states. The Rademacher Standard requires complete dependency visibility, no hidden inferential compression, explicit necessity and sufficiency statements, and parallel mathematical and prose exposition. CDPI and Realization Mechanism Neutrality require the program to distinguish architectural invariants from the mechanisms through which they are measured or realized. 
Established methods used here include preregistration, temporal holdout, benchmark comparison, reliability analysis, proper scoring, survival analysis, sequential testing, cumulative evidence synthesis, and reproducible reporting. Their application to live relational systems is a recontextualization of existing empirical methodology. The framework-specific contribution is the prospective demonstration architecture connecting these methods to compatibility, recovery, pressure, representation, legitimacy, resonance, reachability, obstruction horizons, admissible endpoint geometry, and recursive failure-shape learning. 
3.14.11.2 Program Objects and Temporal Semantics 
Definition 3.14.11.1 (Prospective Demonstration) 
D = (Ω₀, 𝔐, B, G, P, F, W, Ω₁, S, A, Q).
Here Ω₀ is the frozen pre-outcome information state; 𝔐 is the signed measurement contract; B is the locked benchmark family; G is the locked ICG reconstruction; P is the prediction family; F is the falsifier family; W = (t₀,t₁] is the outcome window; Ω₁ is the outcome record unavailable at registration; S is the scoring and adjudication architecture; A is the admissibility architecture; and Q is the immutable provenance and version record. 
Definition 3.14.11.2 (Genuine Prospectivity) 
Pros(D)=1 ⇔ Ω₁ ∉ σ(Ω₀,𝔐,B,G,P,F,S,A,Q) at t₀.
The symbol σ denotes the information generated by its arguments. Genuine prospectivity requires that neither the outcome nor a leakage-equivalent proxy enters the registered derivation before t₁. 
Definition 3.14.11.3 (Demonstration Status) 
Status(D) ∈ {registered, active, completed, supported, contradicted, unresolved, protocol-invalid, retired}. 
The statuses supported, contradicted, and unresolved apply to registered claims. Protocol-invalid applies when the prospective information firewall, measurement contract, or adjudication procedure fails. Retired applies when the relevant claim family has no remaining admissible revision path. 
Theorem 3.14.11.1 (Prospective Demonstration Integrity Theorem) 
If Pros(D)=1, all transformations are locked at t₀, deviations are fully logged, and Ω₁ is adjudicated only after t₁ under S, then the documented prediction family P is temporally prior to the evaluated outcome. 
Proof 
By Definition 3.14.11.2, Ω₁ is absent from the information generating P at registration. Locking prevents post-registration alteration of the predictive map. Delayed adjudication prevents outcome-dependent relabeling. Therefore the documented dependency graph contains no path from Ω₁ to P. Any leakage, unlogged alteration, or outcome-dependent relabeling violates a premise and changes the study status to protocol-invalid. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem establishes procedural prospectivity, not truth, adequate power, or transportability. 
3.14.11.3 Endpoint Geometry and Demonstration Admissibility 
A prospective demonstration must align with a declared endpoint geometry. The endpoint is not a privileged winning demonstration. It is the structural shape that a candidate must inhabit in order to test a declared claim without violating scientific, ethical, or governance constraints. 
Definition 3.14.11.4 (Demonstration Endpoint Geometry) 
Eᴰ = (Y, H, U, Rₑ, Lₑ, Cₑ),
where Y is the measurable target relation, H is the horizon, U is the unit and level of analysis, Rₑ is the required evidentiary resolution, Lₑ is the logical claim strength, and Cₑ is the consequence class whose observation would support, contradict, or leave unresolved the target claim. 
Definition 3.14.11.5 (Demonstration Admissibility Architecture) 
Aᴰ = Aᶜ ∩ Aᵐ ∩ Aᵇ ∩ Aᵉ ∩ Aˡ ∩ Aʳ ∩ Aᵖ ∩ Aᵛ ∩ Aᶠ,
where the factors require, respectively: claim compatibility, measurable outcomes, benchmark availability, ethical admissibility, legitimacy, representation, privacy and safety, viable execution, and finite evaluability. A candidate demonstration d is admissible exactly when d ∈ Aᴰ and its predicted consequence class aligns with Eᴰ. 
Definition 3.14.11.6 (Surviving Demonstration Field) 
𝒟* = {d ∈ 𝒟 : d aligns with Eᴰ and L_A(d)=∅}.
The admissibility-loss object L_A(d) is the set of violated conditions. The program returns the full field 𝒟*. It does not select among multiple surviving demonstrations. If |𝒟*|=1, the unique survivor may be instantiated without an additional selection operation. If |𝒟*|>1, consequences are characterized and the researcher or authorized participants select among the survivors. 
Theorem 3.14.11.2 (Demonstration Filtering Theorem) 
The program’s canonical selection operation is elimination of candidates that fail endpoint alignment or admissibility; it is not winner selection among surviving candidates. 
Proof 
By Definition 3.14.11.6, membership in 𝒟* depends only on endpoint alignment and the absence of admissibility violations. No utility maximum, regret-to-best quantity, or kernel-selected winner appears. Hence the operation maps a candidate field to a surviving admissible field. A singular output occurs only when filtering itself leaves one element. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This theorem incorporates the kernel review rule that forbids hidden winner-selection after admissibility filtering. 
3.14.11.4 Registration and Dependency Architecture 
Definition 3.14.11.7 (Demonstration Registry Entry) 
ρᴰ = (id, claim, Ω₀, assumptions, 𝔐, B, G, P, F, W, S, Aᴰ, Q).
Every field is mandatory. Observations, ordinary inferences, ICG reconstructions, and predictions must occupy distinct typed blocks. A version change creates a descendant registration and never overwrites its ancestor. 
Block 
Required content 
Failure excluded

Theorem 3.14.11.3 (Registry Completeness Theorem) 
A demonstration lacking any dependency required to determine its claim, forecast, falsifier, admissibility, or score is not confirmatory. 
Proof 
A confirmatory result requires a finite auditable map from evidence through measurement and reconstruction to prediction and adjudication. If a required dependency is absent, at least one inferential transition remains unconstrained and may be filled after outcome observation. Therefore the demonstration cannot satisfy prospective accountability and must be classified exploratory or protocol-incomplete. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
Completeness protects against narrative flexibility while retaining exploratory work as hypothesis generation. 
3.14.11.5 Demonstration Family I: Hidden Recoverability 
Definition 3.14.11.8 (Registered Hidden-Recoverability Claim) 
HR(x₀,H)=1 ⇔ ∃γ=(x₀,…,xₖ), k≤H, such that γ∈𝒯* and xₖ∈R.
The trajectory γ must satisfy declared compatibility, legitimacy, representation, pressure, resilience, safety, and future-optionality constraints. The claim concerns existence of at least one admissible corridor, not selection of a preferred corridor and not mere endpoint improvement. 
Definition 3.14.11.9 (Hidden-Recoverability Falsifier) 
For a finite state or sufficiently identified transition system, the strong falsifier is proof that no admissible path from x₀ reaches R within H. In open systems, nonobservation alone is generally weak evidence because an admissible but unrealized path may remain. 
Theorem 3.14.11.4 (Hidden-Recoverability Identifiability Theorem) 
A positive hidden-recoverability claim is strongly testable only when admissible transitions are sufficiently observed, intervened upon, or formally verified to establish corridor existence; a negative claim requires sufficient transition completeness to exclude all admissible corridors. 
Proof 
The positive claim is existential and is established by one verified admissible corridor. The negative claim is universal over candidate corridors and therefore requires exclusion of each admissible possibility. In incomplete open systems, failure to realize a corridor does not prove its absence. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The asymmetry is inherited from reachability mathematics and prevents nonselection from being confused with impossibility. 
3.14.11.6 Demonstration Family II: False Recovery 
Definition 3.14.11.10 (Registered Structural Recovery) 
Recᴰ = Perf↑ ∧ Obs↓ ∧ Reach↑ ∧ Resil↑ ∧ Leg=1 ∧ Rep=1 over Wᴰ.
The terms denote preregistered operational measures of performance, governing obstruction, reachable admissible futures, resilience, legitimacy, and representation across a durability window Wᴰ. Domain-specific measurement contracts must replace the symbolic placeholders before registration. 
Definition 3.14.11.11 (False-Recovery Candidate) 
FRᶜ = Perf↑ ∧ ¬(Obs↓ ∨ Bypass_adm ∨ ConstraintResolution).
A candidate becomes a validated false recovery only if the registered durability criterion fails, recurrence occurs, or the reachable admissible landscape contracts as predicted. Apparent improvement alone is insufficient. 
Theorem 3.14.11.5 (False-Recovery Disconfirmation Theorem) 
A false-recovery prediction is contradicted when durable structural recovery persists through Wᴰ while the registered obstruction remains unchanged, no admissible bypass is detected, and measurement invariance holds. 
Proof 
The prediction asserts that unresolved obstruction prevents durable recovery. Persistence under the conjunction of unchanged obstruction, absent bypass, and invariant measurement realizes the registered incompatible consequence. Therefore at least the obstruction reconstruction, its claimed necessity, or its measurement must be revised. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem makes false recovery a risky prospective claim rather than a label applied after recurrence. 
3.14.11.7 Demonstration Family III: Obstruction Horizon 
Definition 3.14.11.12 (Obstruction-Horizon Process) 
Hₒ(t) = (Pᶜ(t), Θᴮ(t), μ(Reach_A(xₜ)), Res(t), Leg(t), Rep(t), Uᴿ(t)).
The components denote compatibility pressure, boundary reserve or thickness, measure of the admissible reachable landscape, resonance, legitimacy, representation, and unrealized compatibility. Numerical use requires validated measurement contracts; otherwise the process remains ordinal. 
Definition 3.14.11.13 (Registered Alarm) 
Aₒ(t)=1{g(Hₒ(t))≥τₒ},
where g, threshold τₒ, target event, lead-time interval, and false-alarm burden are calibrated without outcome-window access and frozen at registration. 
Theorem 3.14.11.6 (Obstruction-Horizon Incremental Warning Theorem) 
A registered obstruction-horizon process demonstrates incremental early-warning value only if it improves the locked benchmark score or decision-relevant lead-time performance under the registered false-alarm constraint. 
Proof 
An alarm that precedes an event may do so by frequent firing. Benchmark parity, fixed event semantics, and a false-alarm constraint remove that trivial explanation. Improvement under identical evidence therefore demonstrates task-relative information contributed by the registered ICG geometry. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The conclusion is local to the tested system, horizon, and realization mechanism unless CDPI transport conditions are separately established. 
3.14.11.8 Demonstration Family IV: Latent Diversity Activation 
Definition 3.14.11.14 (Latent Diversity Reserve) 
Dᴸ(x₀)= {r : r is represented in the latent relation architecture but inactive in the realized configuration at t₀}.
The object is a set or structured field of unrealized relational capacities, not an invented scalar. A scalar summary may be introduced only through a declared measure preserving the relevant structure. 
Definition 3.14.11.15 (Activation Claim) 
Act(Dᴸ,a,H)=1 ⇔ μ(Reach_A(x_H | a)) > μ(Reach_A(x₀)) and ND(a)=1,
where intervention a is admissible, ND requires non-domination, and the comparison concerns expansion of the admissible reachable landscape. The program does not require or authorize selection of one future from that expanded landscape. 
Theorem 3.14.11.7 (Latent-Diversity Activation Theorem) 
A prospective latent-diversity claim is supported only when preregistered latent relations become operational through an admissible intervention and produce a registered expansion or restructuring of the admissible reachable landscape beyond benchmark expectation. 
Proof 
Visible improvement may arise without latent-diversity activation. The claim specifically concerns preidentified latent relations, their activation through a, and a consequent reachable-landscape change. All three dependencies must be observed or independently verified. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This separates latent diversity from post hoc attribution of any beneficial change to hidden capacity. 
3.14.11.9 Comparative and Ablation Demonstrations 
Definition 3.14.11.16 (Paired Prospective Comparison) 
Cᴰ=(Ω₀,B(Ω₀),G(Ω₀),Ω₁,S).
Benchmark and ICG models receive identical frozen evidence and are evaluated on identical withheld outcomes under the same score. The benchmark portfolio must be the strongest reasonable family available at t₀, not a deliberately weak comparator. 
Definition 3.14.11.17 (Projection Ablation Family) 
G⁻ʲ = G with projection j removed, j∈{boundary,recovery,pressure,representation,legitimacy,resonance,reachability}.
Ablations test incremental empirical contribution. Failure of a projection to improve prediction in one task does not prove the projection mathematically false; it restricts its demonstrated predictive contribution at the tested resolution. 
Theorem 3.14.11.8 (Fair Comparative Demonstration Theorem) 
If B and G use identical Ω₀, remain locked through W, and G achieves a preregistered, uncertainty-qualified improvement under S, then G contributes prospective information not captured by B for that task. 
Proof 
The identical evidence condition excludes informational privilege. Locked models exclude outcome-driven revision. The shared proper or task-appropriate score makes the comparison commensurable. A qualified improvement therefore arises from registered model structure or estimation. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
No universal superiority follows from one domain or one realization mechanism. 
3.14.11.10 Calibration Metrics under Admissible-Landscape Geometry 
Calibration metrics must evaluate predictive correspondence without smuggling a winner-selection geometry into trajectory assessment. Probability calibration, event discrimination, interval coverage, set coverage, and lead-time error remain admissible because they compare registered predictions with outcomes. Regret-to-best is excluded because it collapses a surviving field to a privileged trajectory and transfers post-filter selection to the model. 
Definition 3.14.11.18 (Admissible-Set Coverage) 
Cov_A = |R_obs ∩ R̂_A| / |R_obs|,
where R̂_A is the predicted admissible reachable set and R_obs is the set of verified realized states or trajectories within the evaluation window. Coverage must be accompanied by a false-inclusion audit because enlarging R̂_A trivially increases coverage. 
Definition 3.14.11.19 (Admissibility-Violation Profile) 
L_A(γ) = {c∈Γ_A : c(γ)=0}.
For each candidate trajectory, the profile records violated constraints. For a predicted surviving field 𝒯* and verified outcome trajectory γ_obs, evaluation asks whether γ_obs was retained when admissible, excluded when inadmissible, and assigned the correct violation profile. It does not ask whether the kernel chose the same winner as an ex post utility maximizer. 
Definition 3.14.11.20 (Surviving-Field Precision) 
Prec_A = |𝒯* ∩ 𝒯_valid| / |𝒯*|,
where 𝒯_valid is the set of trajectories independently verified to satisfy the registered endpoint and admissibility architecture. When exhaustive verification is impossible, bounds and unresolved classifications must replace false completeness. 
Theorem 3.14.11.9 (Winner-Free Calibration Theorem) 
Admissible trajectory evaluation can be calibrated through set inclusion, exclusion, coverage, violation-profile accuracy, and consequence prediction without defining or selecting a singular best trajectory. 
Proof 
Each listed metric compares a predicted structural object—membership, exclusion, constraint profile, or consequence class—with verified observations. None requires a total ordering or model-selected winner. Hence empirical evaluation is possible while preserving the full surviving field and user selection authority. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This theorem replaces decision regret with metrics aligned to filtering-by-elimination. 
3.14.11.11 Multi-Domain Registry and Cumulative Evidence 
Definition 3.14.11.21 (Prospective Demonstration Registry) 
ℛᴰ = {ρᴰ₁,ρᴰ₂,…}.
The registry preserves every registration, version, deviation, null result, contradiction, unresolved result, and protocol-invalid study. Deletion or selective publication is inadmissible. 
Definition 3.14.11.22 (Cumulative Evidence State) 
Eₙ = (D₁,…,Dₙ; Q₁,…,Qₙ; T₁,…,Tₙ),
where Dᵢ is the study result, Qᵢ its quality and protocol status, and Tᵢ its transport domain. Aggregation must respect dependence, heterogeneity, outcome semantics, and architecture-relative validity. 
Theorem 3.14.11.10 (Cumulative Evidence Non-Collapse Theorem) 
The evidential state of the program cannot be reduced to the count of supported demonstrations without loss of validity-relevant structure. 
Proof 
Studies differ in quality, independence, domain, measurement, claim class, and transportability. A success count discards these relations and permits many weak dependent studies to dominate fewer strong contradictory studies. Therefore cumulative evidence must preserve study-level structure or use an aggregation rule that explicitly models it. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem prevents validation from becoming a winner-election among study outcomes. 
3.14.11.12 CDPI and Realization-Mechanism-Neutral Demonstration 
Definition 3.14.11.23 (Realization Mechanism Frame) 
F_RM(D) = (Architecture, Mechanism, Measurement, Environment).
Architectural truth concerns structural relations retained across admissible mechanisms. Mechanism-relative truth concerns the performance of a particular operational realization. Environment-relative truth concerns the tested population, constraints, and transition laws. 
Definition 3.14.11.24 (Cross-Domain Portability Test) 
A structural claim satisfies a tested CDPI instance when an explicitly defined invariant relation is preserved across at least two non-equivalent domains or realization mechanisms under registered transport conditions. 
Theorem 3.14.11.11 (Realization Non-Substitution Theorem) 
Success of one realization mechanism does not prove the architecture realization-independent, and failure of one mechanism does not refute the architecture unless the failed property is mechanism-invariant. 
Proof 
A realized outcome is generated jointly by architecture, mechanism, measurement, and environment. Without an invariance proof or cross-mechanism test, the contributions are not identified. Therefore conclusions must remain relative to F_RM. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This protects both against overclaiming from success and overgeneralizing from local failure. 
3.14.11.13 Representation, Legitimacy, and Participant Authority 
A live demonstration acts on or observes participants. Scientific value does not override their authority, privacy, contestability, or viable exit. The program therefore requires separate epistemic and admissibility review. 
Definition 3.14.11.25 (Participant-Admissible Demonstration) 
PartAdm(D)=Consent ∧ Representation ∧ Contestability ∧ Privacy ∧ Safety ∧ ViableExit ∧ Review.
The operational meaning of each factor must be defined for the domain. Consent is not sufficient when refusal is nonviable or when materially affected nonparticipants bear the consequences. 
Theorem 3.14.11.12 (Epistemic–Legitimacy Independence Theorem) 
Predictive accuracy neither entails participant legitimacy nor compensates for its absence. 
Proof 
Accuracy is a relation between forecasts and outcomes. Legitimacy is a relation among authority, participation, justification, contestability, and exit. Neither definition entails the other. Therefore both must be satisfied independently before deployment is admissible. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The program may study an accurate but inadmissible model under appropriate safeguards; it may not infer deployment legitimacy from accuracy. 
3.14.11.14 Recursive Error-Shape Learning and Kernel Review 
Definition 3.14.11.26 (Failure-Shape Extraction) 
Φ_err : e ↦ Shape(Localize(e)),
where e is an identified error, hallucination, invalid inference, hindsight contamination, category collapse, hidden winner selection, or protocol failure. Φ_err removes wording- and domain-specific realization details while preserving the dependency relation that generated the failure. 
Definition 3.14.11.27 (Inadmissible Shape Archive) 
𝔉⁻ₙ₊₁ = 𝔉⁻ₙ ∪ {Φ_err(eₙ₊₁)}.
Two errors are shape-equivalent when their dependency and transformation relations are isomorphic at the review resolution, even if their words, symbols, domains, or realization mechanisms differ. 
Definition 3.14.11.28 (Kernel Review Filter) 
K_rev(ρ)=admissible ⇔ ∄F∈𝔉⁻ such that Shape(ρ) ≅ F,
unless a declared structural distinction breaks the isomorphism and is independently justified. The archive currently includes at least hindsight contamination, observation–reconstruction collapse, and winner-selection after multiple admissible survivors. 
Theorem 3.14.11.13 (Recursive Error-Shape Learning Theorem) 
If a detected failure is correctly localized, reconstructed into an invariant relational shape, archived, and applied to future dependency graphs, then future realizations of the same shape become filterable independently of their terminology or domain. 
Proof 
Correct localization identifies the generating relation. Shape reconstruction removes incidental realization details while preserving that relation. Archiving makes the relation available to future review. Structural comparison detects isomorphic reoccurrences. Therefore the corrective dependency no longer rests on repeated wording. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
This is recursive shape-learning, not autonomous modification of the underlying model. Its validity depends on correct localization, suitable review resolution, and continued audit of false shape matches. 
3.14.11.15 Failure, Revision, and Research-Program Recovery 
Definition 3.14.11.29 (Demonstration Failure Localization) 
Loc(D)=min ancestor v in Dep(D) whose registered claim is contradicted or whose protocol condition fails.
The minimum is taken relative to dependency depth from the failed output. Candidate locations include measurement, data provenance, assumption, reconstruction, prediction map, transport condition, admissibility rule, and protocol execution. 
Definition 3.14.11.30 (Admissible Revision Field) 
Rev*(v)= {r : r repairs v, preserves unaffected dependencies, survives Aᴰ, and creates a new prospective registration}.
The program returns the complete surviving revision field. It does not select among multiple revisions. Researchers choose among the characterized survivors; a unique survivor may be returned directly. 
Theorem 3.14.11.14 (Research-Program Recovery Theorem) 
Failure of one demonstration invalidates the entire framework only when failure localizes to a dependency required by every admissible realization and the corresponding admissible revision field is empty. 
Proof 
By dependency locality, a failed output first implicates its ancestors. If the failed ancestor is not universal, unaffected branches remain. If a nonempty admissible revision field exists, unrealized compatibility remains positive and a new prospective test is possible. Global invalidation follows only when the failed dependency is universal and no admissible repair survives. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The research program applies pathway-recovery architecture to itself without converting revision into retrospective rescue. 
3.14.11.16 Minimal Operational Algorithm 
The prospective demonstration program shall execute the following realization-neutral sequence: 
Declare the endpoint geometry, claim class, unit, horizon, and consequence classes. 
Construct the candidate demonstration landscape from domains with finite observability. 
Apply endpoint alignment and scientific, ethical, legitimacy, representation, privacy, safety, and feasibility constraints. 
Return the full surviving demonstration field; if multiple candidates survive, preserve user selection authority. 
For the selected demonstration, freeze observations, measurement contracts, benchmarks, ICG reconstruction, predictions, falsifiers, scores, stopping rules, and provenance hashes. 
Run kernel review against the inadmissible shape archive before activation. 
Open the blinded outcome window; prohibit model revision and log interventions or safety-mandated unblinding. 
Reveal outcomes only after the registered horizon and adjudicate under the locked rules. 
Evaluate calibration, discrimination, set coverage, violation profiles, comparative performance, legitimacy, and transport limits. 
Classify each claim as supported, contradicted, unresolved, or protocol-invalid. 
Localize failures, reconstruct their geometric shapes, update the inadmissible archive, and generate the full admissible revision field. 
Publish all registrations, deviations, outcomes, null results, contradictions, and revisions. 
3.14.11.17 Prospective Demonstration Program Theorem 
Theorem 3.14.11.15 (Prospective Demonstration Program Soundness Theorem) 
Assume each demonstration satisfies the registration, information-firewall, measurement, benchmark, falsification, admissibility, participant-governance, kernel-review, and reporting conditions defined above. Then the program generates a cumulative, auditable, realization-mechanism-aware body of evidence in which supported, contradicted, unresolved, and invalid results remain distinguishable and scientifically actionable. 
Proof 
Registration and the temporal firewall establish prospectivity. Measurement contracts and typed dependencies establish traceability. Benchmarks and locked scores establish comparative interpretability. Falsifiers expose predictions to contradiction. Admissibility and participant-governance conditions prevent predictive accuracy from substituting for legitimacy. Kernel review filters archived failure shapes. Complete reporting prevents selective survival. Failure localization and admissible revision fields make contradiction scientifically actionable without automatic global collapse. Therefore the cumulative archive preserves the distinctions required for sound program-level inference. 
∎ 
Interpretation 
The theorem establishes architectural soundness conditional on faithful execution. It does not assert that ICG predictions will succeed. 
3.14.11.18 Dependency, Provenance, and Contribution Map 
3.14.7 measurement → 3.14.8 realization → 3.14.9 historical firewall → 3.14.10 prospective accountability → 3.14.11 live cumulative program.
Established mathematics and empirical practice provide temporal holdout, set-valued prediction, reachability asymmetry, calibration, proper scoring, reliability, survival analysis, reproducibility, and cumulative evidence methods. The present section newly applies those methods to live ICG demonstrations. The distinctive structures introduced here are the endpoint-aligned surviving demonstration field, winner-free calibration family, cross-mechanism demonstration frame, participant-admissible demonstration condition, recursive error-shape learning operator, inadmissible shape archive, kernel review filter, and admissible revision field. 
The section depends on the Compatibility Kernel inheritance chain Inh→SC→Pers→Rec→SL; the pathway-recovery distinction among objective, selector, pathway, and realization; CDPI; the Realization Mechanism Frame F_RM; and the standing rule that projection returns a surviving admissible structure rather than a model-selected winner. 
3.14.11.19 Conditions Requiring Restriction, Revision, or Retirement 
The program must restrict, revise, or retire the relevant claim family when prospective evidence establishes any of the following: 
core constructs cannot be measured with adequate reliability or architecture-relative invariance; 
prediction families repeatedly enter preregistered strong falsifier sets; 
ICG adds no prospective information beyond strong benchmarks in adequately powered tasks; 
hidden-recoverability or reachability claims remain unidentifiable because transition completeness cannot be achieved; 
false-recovery or obstruction-horizon claims require outcome-dependent definitions; 
cross-domain claims fail CDPI tests and no narrower invariant survives; 
participant legitimacy, representation, privacy, safety, or viable exit constraints cannot be satisfied; 
a failure localizes to a universal dependency and Rev*(v)=∅; 
kernel review repeatedly identifies an archived inadmissible geometry that cannot be removed without destroying the claim. 
No contradicted claim may be rescued by changing its target, horizon, score, admissibility conditions, or endpoint geometry after unblinding. Every revision begins a new prospective lineage. 
3.14.11.20 Conclusion and Transition 
Section 3.14.10 established that ICG can be made prospectively accountable. The present section establishes the complete research-program architecture through which that accountability becomes live, cumulative, realization-mechanism-aware, and recursively corrigible. The program does not make the framework infallible. It makes error visible, localizable, shape-reconstructible, and reusable as a future filter. 
The central geometric progression is 
Candidate demonstrations → endpoint geometry → admissibility filtering → surviving demonstration field → user-authorized instantiation → blinded outcome → adjudication → failure-shape learning → revised surviving field. 
The next admissible treatise trajectories are therefore structurally distinct. One trajectory instantiates the first live registered demonstration. Another proceeds to Chapter 3.15 Emergence while subjecting future emergence claims to the prospective machinery now established. The mathematics does not select between multiple surviving trajectories; it returns their consequences and preserves participant selection. If the declared endpoint is immediate empirical instantiation, the first trajectory aligns directly. If the declared endpoint is continued theorem development before live execution, the emergence trajectory remains available, but its future claims inherit all registration, falsification, CDPI, and kernel-review obligations established here. 
3.14.12 First Registered Demonstration Candidate Landscape
Purpose
Sections 3.14.9–3.14.11 established, respectively:
a historical validation architecture,
a prospective validation and falsification architecture,
a prospective demonstration architecture capable of producing admissible future empirical evidence.
A natural question therefore arises.
Which demonstrations should actually enter the prospective demonstration program?
The purpose of the present section is to construct the complete admissible landscape of prospective demonstrations capable of testing the Compatibility–ICG architecture. The objective is not the selection of a privileged demonstration. The objective is the construction of the admissible demonstration landscape itself. The framework therefore performs four operations:
identification of candidate demonstration domains,
construction of the admissibility architecture governing demonstrations,
elimination of inadmissible candidates,
characterization of the surviving admissible demonstration landscape.
The framework does not select among multiple surviving admissible demonstrations. Selection remains external to the mathematical architecture and is the responsibility of the researcher or authorized participant. The section therefore extends the projection methodology previously established. Just as trajectory analysis proceeds through:
Candidate Trajectory Landscape
↓
Admissibility Constraints
↓
Surviving Admissible Landscape
prospective validation proceeds through:
Candidate Demonstration Landscape
↓
Demonstration Admissibility Constraints
↓
Surviving Demonstration Landscape
The resulting landscape becomes the admissible domain from which future demonstrations may be chosen.
3.14.12.1 Motivation
Objective
The preceding section established how prospective demonstrations must be conducted. The next question is:
Which demonstrations are actually admissible?
The answer is not obvious. A candidate demonstration may appear attractive while failing to satisfy one or more requirements necessary for meaningful prospective validation. For example, a candidate demonstration may:
lack sufficiently observable outcomes,
lack adequate measurement structure,
lack benchmark comparators,
fail representation or legitimacy requirements,
fail ethical admissibility constraints,
admit no meaningful falsifiers,
produce no recoverable information regardless of outcome.
Consequently not every possible demonstration possesses equal scientific value.  The determination of viable demonstrations therefore becomes a problem of admissibility rather than preference. The Compatibility–ICG framework asks:
Which demonstrations survive the declared endpoint geometry and admissibility architecture?
rather than:
Which demonstration appears most interesting?
This distinction is essential. Interest is not an admissibility criterion. Convenience is not an admissibility criterion. Researcher preference is not an admissibility criterion. The framework instead requires that every candidate demonstration satisfy the prospectively accountable validation architecture developed in Section 3.14.10.
Architectural Observation
A common research pattern follows the geometry:
Candidate Demonstrations
↓
Researcher Preference
↓
Chosen Demonstration
The Compatibility–ICG framework treats this geometry as incomplete. The act of selecting a single demonstration before evaluating admissibility introduces the same structural compression that motivated the framework's rejection of winner-selection architectures elsewhere. The preferred geometry is:
Candidate Demonstrations
↓
Declared Endpoint Geometry
↓
Admissibility Constraints
↓
Filtering and Elimination
↓
Surviving Demonstration Landscape
The surviving landscape constitutes the primary mathematical object. Selection, if required, occurs only after the admissible landscape has been identified. Consequently the framework preserves all surviving admissible candidates together with their respective consequences, limitations, risks, validation horizons, measurement requirements, and future-reaching implications.
Dependency Structure
The present section depends upon the following previously established developments:
reachability geometry from Section 3.14.4,
comparative architecture from Section 3.14.6,
measurement architecture from Section 3.14.7,
computational realization architecture from Section 3.14.8,
historical validation architecture from Section 3.14.9,
prospective validation architecture from Section 3.14.10,
the kernel rule that treats winner-selection geometries as inadmissible,
the endpoint-geometry and admissibility-filtering methodology of the Compatibility Kernel.
The section therefore represents the first direct application of the complete validation architecture to the future trajectory of the research program itself.
Program-Level Interpretation
The Compatibility–ICG architecture is now sufficiently developed that future advancement of the framework should increasingly proceed through evidence-generating trajectories whenever possible. Mathematical development remains important. However, the presently declared endpoint geometry is no longer merely:
Expand the theoretical architecture.
The endpoint geometry now includes:
empirical accountability,
prospective prediction,
falsification exposure,
cumulative evidence production,
recursive correction and revision.
The framework therefore treats candidate demonstrations as future evidence-producing trajectories. The present section asks:
Which such trajectories survive admissibility filtering?
The answer to that question is the object developed throughout the remainder of the section:
the First Registered Demonstration Candidate Landscape.
3.14.12.2 Demonstration Universe
The prospective demonstration program established in Section 3.14.11 requires a mathematically explicit characterization of the domains upon which the Compatibility–ICG architecture may be tested. The objective of the present subsection is therefore not to identify a preferred demonstration, nor to justify the selection of any particular future study. Rather, the objective is to construct the universe of candidate demonstrations and to establish the formal conditions under which a candidate becomes an admissible member of the demonstration landscape.
The mathematical structures employed in this subsection are largely established. State spaces, measurable outcomes, observation architectures, governance structures, and evaluation horizons all possess extensive antecedents in statistics, systems engineering, operations research, experimental design, and empirical science. The distinctive contribution introduced here is the construction of a common domain representation capable of supporting Compatibility Geometry, Recovery Geometry, Reachability Geometry, Resonance Geometry, Pressure Geometry, Representation Geometry, Legitimacy Geometry, and their associated validation architectures within a single evaluative object.
Definition 3.14.12.1 (Demonstration Domain)
A demonstration domain is an ordered quintuple
D = (O, Y, W, M, G)
where:
O denotes the observation architecture;
Y denotes the measurable outcome architecture;
W denotes the outcome horizon;
M denotes the measurement architecture;
G denotes the governance architecture.
Each component serves a distinct role.
The observation architecture O contains all admissible information available at the beginning of the demonstration. These observations may consist of measurements, records, events, behavioral traces, surveys, operational logs, organizational reports, state variables, or any other observational structures supplied to the prospective demonstration.
The measurable outcome architecture Y specifies the class of future observations against which predictions will be evaluated. Outcomes must be observable, operationalizable, and capable of independent verification. Examples include recovery events, failures, performance transitions, coordination outcomes, organizational restructurings, innovation measures, governance changes, resilience outcomes, or other registered consequence classes. The outcome horizon W specifies the temporal interval over which validation occurs. Formally,
W = (t₀, t₁]
where t₀ denotes registration time and t₁ denotes outcome evaluation time. The measurement architecture M specifies how observations and outcomes are transformed into empirical quantities. This includes operational definitions, scales, units, estimation procedures, uncertainty characterization, reliability requirements, missing-data procedures, and admissibility rules governing measurement itself.
The governance architecture G specifies the authority structure under which the demonstration operates. Governance includes participant representation, legitimacy conditions, consent structures, auditing requirements, contestability procedures, revision authority, privacy constraints, admissibility conditions, and the institutional structure responsible for maintaining the validity of the demonstration.
The demonstration domain therefore combines empirical, temporal, measurement, and governance structures into a single mathematical object.
Interpretation
A demonstration domain is not merely a dataset.
A demonstration domain is not merely a prediction target.
A demonstration domain is not merely an outcome window.
Rather, a demonstration domain represents the complete environment within which a prospective validation task becomes meaningful.
This distinction is essential because predictions are never evaluated in isolation. Predictions exist within systems of observation, measurement, governance, representation, legitimacy, and temporal evolution. The demonstration domain is therefore the smallest object capable of supporting prospective accountability.
Definition 3.14.12.2 (Candidate Demonstration Universe)
Let
𝒟
denote the collection of all prospective demonstration domains satisfying Definition 3.14.12.1. The collection 𝒟 is called the candidate demonstration universe. An element
D ∈ 𝒟
need not yet be admissible. Membership in 𝒟 requires only that the object possesses well-defined observation, outcome, horizon, measurement, and governance architectures. The purpose of subsequent admissibility filtering is to determine which elements of 𝒟 survive the constraints established by the Compatibility–ICG validation architecture.
Candidate Demonstration Classes
The candidate demonstration universe includes a wide variety of domains. Examples include:
Software Projects
A software project constitutes a demonstration domain if:
observations can be collected during development,
outcomes such as completion, adoption, failure, defect emergence, recovery, or architectural evolution are measurable,
a validation horizon exists,
measurement procedures can be defined,
governance and participation structures are identified.
Software projects are particularly attractive because they often possess rich observational records and relatively short validation horizons.
Open-Source Communities
Open-source communities provide naturally occurring interoperability environments. Observations may include:
contribution networks,
communication structures,
issue-resolution histories,
governance transitions,
project adoption trajectories.
Outcomes may include:
project survival,
contributor growth,
fragmentation,
coordination success,
architectural recovery.
These domains are especially useful because many observations are publicly accessible.
Organizational Restructurings
Organizations undergoing structural change frequently exhibit:
compatibility transitions,
recovery opportunities,
governance transformations,
legitimacy changes,
pressure redistribution,
representation shifts.
Such domains provide rich opportunities for observing interoperability geometry directly.
Product Development Efforts
Product-development environments often possess:
explicit objectives,
identifiable pathways,
measurable outcomes,
resource constraints,
recoverability structures.
Consequently they provide natural environments for testing pathway-recovery and reachability architectures.
Governance Transitions
Governance transitions are particularly valuable for:
representation architecture,
legitimacy architecture,
domination analysis,
boundary generation,
compatibility pressure.
The prospective consequences of governance changes are often directly measurable.
Technology Adoption Programs
Technology-adoption processes exhibit:
compatibility barriers,
resonance opportunities,
diversity effects,
adoption thresholds,
reachability constraints.
They therefore provide a useful testing environment for interoperability architectures.
Recovery Programs
Recovery programs are especially relevant because they permit direct evaluation of:
hidden recoverability,
pathway redeployment,
selector ancestry,
obstruction localization,
false-recovery detection.
These domains are often among the most informative validation environments for Compatibility–ICG claims.
Operational Interventions
Operational interventions provide opportunities to compare:
predicted trajectories,
realized trajectories,
admissible trajectories,
filtered interventions,
consequence landscapes.
Such demonstrations directly test the trajectory-generation architecture.
Theorem 3.14.12.3 (Demonstration Universe Sufficiency Theorem)
Every prospective demonstration admissible under the Compatibility–ICG architecture must be representable as an element of the candidate demonstration universe 𝒟.
Proof
Every prospective demonstration requires:
observations,
measurable outcomes,
a validation horizon,
a measurement architecture,
a governance architecture.
These are precisely the components of Definition 3.14.12.1. Therefore every admissible demonstration corresponds to a quintuple
D = (O, Y, W, M, G).
Consequently every admissible demonstration belongs to the candidate demonstration universe 𝒟.
∎
Interpretation
The theorem does not establish that every candidate demonstration is admissible. Rather, it establishes that every admissible demonstration must first appear within the candidate universe. The candidate universe is therefore the landscape upon which admissibility filtering operates. This prepares the way for the subsequent subsection, where the admissibility architecture is introduced and applied to the candidate universe in order to construct the surviving demonstration landscape.
3.14.12.3 Demonstration Admissibility Architecture
The candidate demonstration universe constructed in the preceding subsection is intentionally broad. Membership in the candidate universe merely establishes that a domain possesses observable information, measurable outcomes, a validation horizon, a measurement architecture, and a governance architecture. Membership alone does not establish that a domain is suitable for prospective evaluation of the Compatibility–ICG framework.
The purpose of the present subsection is therefore to introduce the admissibility architecture governing prospective demonstrations. Just as candidate trajectories must survive compatibility, legitimacy, recovery, representation, pressure, and reachability constraints before entering the admissible trajectory landscape, candidate demonstrations must survive a distinct collection of scientific, ethical, observational, and governance constraints before entering the admissible demonstration landscape.
The mathematical notion of constraint satisfaction is well established. The framework-specific contribution introduced here is the construction of a unified admissibility architecture for scientific demonstrations, together with the explicit integration of measurement, representation, legitimacy, recoverability, and validation requirements into a common filtering structure.
Definition 3.14.12.4 (Demonstration Admissibility)
Let
D ∈ 𝒟
be a candidate demonstration domain. Let
Γᴰ
denote the collection of admissibility constraints governing prospective demonstrations. Define the admissibility loss of D by
Lᴬ(D) = { c ∈ Γᴰ : c(D)=0 }.
The candidate domain D is admissible if and only if
Lᴬ(D)=∅.
Equivalently, D is admissible precisely when it satisfies every admissibility condition contained in Γᴰ.
Interpretation
This definition introduces no concept of a preferred demonstration. The object of the architecture is not the selection of a single optimal candidate. The object is the elimination of inadmissible candidates. The admissible landscape is therefore generated through filtering rather than through competitive ranking. A candidate domain survives because it violates no admissibility condition. A candidate domain is eliminated because at least one admissibility condition fails.
Definition 3.14.12.5 (Demonstration Admissibility Architecture)
Let
Γᴰ = Γᴹ ∩ Γᴮ ∩ Γᴱ ∩ Γᴿ ∩ Γᴸ ∩ Γᴾ ∩ Γᴼ ∩ Γⱽ
where:
Γᴹ denotes measurement-feasibility constraints,
Γᴮ denotes benchmark-feasibility constraints,
Γᴱ denotes ethical-admissibility constraints,
Γᴿ denotes representation constraints,
Γᴸ denotes legitimacy constraints,
Γᴾ denotes privacy and participant-protection constraints,
Γᴼ denotes outcome-observability constraints,
Γⱽ denotes validation-feasibility constraints.
A candidate demonstration domain must satisfy every component architecture simultaneously.
Definition 3.14.12.6 (Measurement Feasibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies measurement feasibility if:
the required quantities admit operational definitions;
observations can be collected;
measurement procedures are reproducible;
uncertainty can be characterized;
missing-data handling can be defined.
Symbolically,
Γᴹ(D)=1
if and only if all measurement conditions are satisfied.
Interpretation
The condition does not require that measurements already exist. It requires that a defensible measurement architecture can be constructed. Without such a structure, future validation becomes impossible irrespective of the quality of the underlying theory.
Definition 3.14.12.7 (Benchmark Feasibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies benchmark feasibility if one or more reasonable comparison architectures can be applied to the same observational record. Examples include:
statistical models,
causal models,
organizational analyses,
network analyses,
resilience analyses,
forecasting architectures.
Symbolically,
Γᴮ(D)=1
if and only if benchmark comparison is possible.
Interpretation
A demonstration incapable of comparison may still be interesting. However, it cannot support comparative claims concerning incremental value. Accordingly, benchmark feasibility is required for prospective evaluation of ICG.
Definition 3.14.12.8 (Ethical Admissibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies ethical admissibility if:
participation is authorized,
foreseeable harms are constrained,
governance procedures are specified,
intervention effects are reviewable,
participant rights are preserved.
Symbolically,
Γᴱ(D)=1.
Interpretation
The framework distinguishes:
predictive validity,
from
admissible deployment.
An observationally informative demonstration may nonetheless be ethically inadmissible. The two questions must remain separate.
Definition 3.14.12.9 (Representation Admissibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies representation admissibility if materially affected participants possess meaningful representational inclusion within the demonstration architecture. Symbolically,
Γᴿ(D)=1.
Interpretation
Representation admissibility extends the representation geometry developed previously. Prospective demonstrations are not exempt from representational concerns merely because they serve scientific objectives.
Definition 3.14.12.10 (Legitimacy Admissibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies legitimacy admissibility if the affected participants possess legitimate pathways for review, contestation, appeal, or withdrawal according to the declared governance architecture. Symbolically,
Γᴸ(D)=1.
Interpretation
Legitimacy concerns governance of the demonstration itself rather than prediction accuracy. A highly accurate demonstration may still fail legitimacy admissibility.
Definition 3.14.12.11 (Privacy Admissibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies privacy admissibility if the required observations can be collected, stored, processed, and interpreted without violating the declared privacy architecture governing the domain. Symbolically,
Γᴾ(D)=1.
Definition 3.14.12.12 (Outcome Observability)
A candidate demonstration satisfies outcome observability if:
outcomes possess operational definitions,
outcomes can be measured,
outcome occurrence is identifiable,
validation can be performed after the horizon closes.
Symbolically,
Γᴼ(D)=1.
Interpretation
Without observable outcomes, prediction cannot be evaluated. Consequently outcome observability is a necessary condition for prospective testing.
Definition 3.14.12.13 (Validation Feasibility)
A candidate demonstration satisfies validation feasibility if:
a prediction registry can be constructed,
falsifiers can be specified,
an outcome window can be defined,
benchmarks can be frozen,
outcome evaluation can occur.
Symbolically,
Γⱽ(D)=1.
Theorem 3.14.12.14 (Demonstration Admissibility Theorem)
A candidate demonstration domain belongs to the admissible demonstration landscape if and only if it satisfies every component of the demonstration admissibility architecture.
Symbolically,
D ∈ 𝒟* ⇔ Γᴰ(D)=1 ⇔ Lᴬ(D)=∅.
Proof
By Definition 3.14.12.5, the admissibility architecture is the intersection of the component constraint architectures. A candidate domain satisfies Γᴰ if and only if it satisfies every component architecture individually. By Definition 3.14.12.4, a candidate is admissible if and only if its admissibility loss is empty. Hence
Γᴰ(D)=1 ⇔ Lᴬ(D)=∅.
Therefore a candidate demonstration belongs to the admissible demonstration landscape precisely when it violates no admissibility condition.
∎
Corollary 3.14.12.15 (Demonstration Filtering Principle)
The canonical operation of the demonstration program is:
𝒟
↓
Γᴰ
↓
𝒟*
where 𝒟* denotes the surviving admissible demonstration landscape.
Proof
Immediate from the Demonstration Admissibility Theorem.
∎
Interpretation
The significance of the theorem is not the use of constraints, which is classical. The framework-specific consequence is the preservation of the entire surviving admissible demonstration landscape. The architecture does not, by itself, select a preferred demonstration. Instead it constructs the admissible field of demonstrations consistent with the declared endpoint geometry and prospective validation architecture. Selection among multiple surviving admissible demonstrations remains an external act performed by the researcher or authorized participant. Only if admissibility filtering leaves a unique surviving demonstration may the framework return a singular result.
3.14.12.4 Demonstration Filtering Theorem
The candidate demonstration universe constructed in Sections 3.14.12.2–3.14.12.3 is intentionally broader than the collection of demonstrations that will ultimately enter the prospective validation program. The existence of a candidate demonstration domain establishes only that observations, outcomes, horizons, measurement structures, and governance structures can be identified. It does not establish that the corresponding demonstration is scientifically admissible, ethically admissible, operationally feasible, or capable of producing meaningful evidence concerning the Compatibility–ICG architecture.
The purpose of the present theorem is therefore to formalize the transition from the candidate landscape to the surviving admissible demonstration landscape.
The mathematical notion of filtering by constraints is established and appears throughout optimization, feasibility analysis, formal verification, constraint satisfaction systems, and scientific study design. The distinctive contribution introduced here is the treatment of demonstration selection as an admissibility-filtering problem rather than a winner-selection problem. Consistent with the broader Compatibility–ICG methodology, the objective is not to identify a preferred demonstration. The objective is to eliminate demonstrations that violate the declared endpoint geometry or the admissibility architecture until only the surviving admissible landscape remains.
Theorem 3.14.12.16 (Demonstration Filtering Theorem)
Let
𝒟
denote the candidate demonstration universe. Let
Γᴰ
denote the demonstration admissibility architecture defined in Section 3.14.12.3. Then the admissible demonstration landscape is given by
𝒟
↓
Γᴰ
↓
𝒟*
where
𝒟*
{ D ∈ 𝒟 : Γᴰ(D)=1 }.
Equivalently,
𝒟*
{ D ∈ 𝒟 : Lᴬ(D)=∅ }.
Thus the admissible demonstration landscape consists precisely of those candidate demonstrations that satisfy every admissibility condition.
Proof
By Definition 3.14.12.4, a candidate demonstration is admissible if and only if its admissibility loss is empty. That is,
Lᴬ(D)=∅.
By Definition 3.14.12.5, the admissibility architecture Γᴰ is the intersection of the component admissibility architectures
Γᴰ
Γᴹ ∩ Γᴮ ∩ Γᴱ ∩ Γᴿ ∩ Γᴸ ∩ Γᴾ ∩ Γᴼ ∩ Γⱽ.
Consequently,
Γᴰ(D)=1
if and only if
Γᴹ(D)=1,
Γᴮ(D)=1,
Γᴱ(D)=1,
Γᴿ(D)=1,
Γᴸ(D)=1,
Γᴾ(D)=1,
Γᴼ(D)=1,
Γⱽ(D)=1.
Every candidate demonstration violating one or more component conditions possesses
Lᴬ(D) ≠ ∅
and is therefore removed from the admissible landscape. Conversely, every candidate satisfying all component conditions possesses
Lᴬ(D)=∅
and survives. Therefore the admissible demonstration landscape is exactly
𝒟*
{ D ∈ 𝒟 : Γᴰ(D)=1 }.
Hence admissibility filtering transforms the candidate universe into the surviving demonstration landscape.
∎
Corollary 3.14.12.17 (Demonstration Elimination Principle)
Every demonstration removed from the admissible landscape is removed because at least one declared admissibility condition fails.
Proof
Immediate from the Demonstration Filtering Theorem.
∎
Interpretation
The framework never eliminates a demonstration merely because another candidate appears stronger. Every elimination must be traceable to a specific admissibility violation.
Consequently the geometry of elimination remains auditable.
Corollary 3.14.12.18 (Admissibility Preservation Principle)
Every demonstration belonging to the admissible landscape satisfies all declared scientific, observational, governance, representation, legitimacy, privacy, and validation conditions.
Proof
Immediate from the definition of Γᴰ and the Demonstration Filtering Theorem.
∎
Corollary 3.14.12.19 (Landscape Preservation Principle)
If
|𝒟*| > 1,
then the framework returns the full admissible demonstration landscape rather than a selected demonstration.
Proof
The Demonstration Filtering Theorem constructs the surviving landscape
𝒟*.
No theorem introduced thus far supplies a rule selecting among multiple admissible survivors. Therefore the framework terminates at the admissible landscape.
∎
Interpretation
This corollary operationalizes one of the central methodological commitments of the Compatibility Kernel. The framework is not a winner-selection architecture. The framework is an admissibility-filtering architecture. Consequently the output of the theorem is not:
the best demonstration,
nor
the preferred demonstration,
nor
the optimal demonstration.
The output is:
the complete surviving admissible demonstration landscape.
The architecture therefore preserves all viable opportunities for future validation rather than collapsing them into a singular recommendation. Only if admissibility filtering yields a unique survivor
|𝒟*| = 1
may the framework return a singular result.
Compatibility–ICG Interpretation
The significance of the theorem is not the use of filtering itself, which is mathematically familiar. The more important contribution is the interaction between filtering and endpoint geometry. The declared endpoint geometry specifies the shape a valid demonstration must inhabit. The admissibility architecture specifies the constraints governing scientific accountability. Demonstration filtering then removes every candidate that fails either condition. Thus the resulting landscape consists of demonstrations that are simultaneously:
scientifically testable,
prospectively accountable,
ethically admissible,
operationally measurable,
representationally valid,
legitimacy preserving,
capable of contributing evidence to the Compatibility–ICG research program.
The theorem therefore transforms the demonstration universe into an admissible evidence-generating landscape and prepares the way for construction of that landscape in the subsequent subsection.
3.14.12.5 Demonstration Consequence Architecture
The admissibility filtering architecture constructed in the preceding subsection determines which candidate demonstrations survive the scientific, observational, legitimacy, representation, privacy, and validation requirements governing the prospective demonstration program. The resulting admissible demonstration landscape identifies which demonstrations may be performed. However, admissibility alone does not determine what each surviving demonstration contributes to the research program.
The purpose of the present subsection is therefore to characterize the informational consequence structure associated with each surviving demonstration domain.
The mathematical ideas employed are largely established. Scientific experiments, observational studies, simulations, and intervention analyses are routinely evaluated according to the information they provide regarding hypotheses, predictions, mechanisms, and outcomes. The framework-specific contribution introduced here is the decomposition of demonstration value into multiple interoperability-geometric consequence layers. This decomposition permits the framework to characterize what each demonstration contributes without introducing a winner-selection architecture among surviving admissible candidates. Consequently the objective is not to identify the best demonstration. The objective is to determine:
What kind of evidence becomes available if a given demonstration is executed?
The resulting structure allows multiple surviving demonstrations to be compared without collapsing the admissible demonstration landscape.
Definition 3.14.12.20 (Demonstration Consequence Architecture)
Let
D ∈ 𝒟*
be an admissible demonstration domain. The demonstration consequence architecture associated with D is the collection
ℭ(D) = (Oᶜ(D), Pᶜ(D), Vᶜ(D), Rᶜ(D), Recᶜ(D), Prᶜ(D))
where:
Oᶜ(D) denotes the observational consequence architecture;
Pᶜ(D) denotes the predictive consequence architecture;
Vᶜ(D) denotes the validation consequence architecture;
Rᶜ(D) denotes the reachability consequence architecture;
Recᶜ(D) denotes the recovery consequence architecture;
Prᶜ(D) denotes the pressure consequence architecture.
The collection ℭ(D) characterizes the future evidence made available through execution of the demonstration.
Interpretation
The admissibility architecture answers:
May this demonstration be performed?
The consequence architecture answers:
What becomes observable if this demonstration is performed?
The two questions are distinct. Multiple demonstrations may remain admissible while producing different classes of evidence. The role of the consequence architecture is to make those distinctions explicit.
Definition 3.14.12.21 (Observational Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Oᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of observations that become available during the execution of the demonstration. Examples include:
state transitions,
participant interactions,
governance behaviors,
constraint activations,
pressure accumulations,
recovery attempts,
interoperability transitions.
Interpretation
The observation layer addresses the question:
What can actually be seen?
Many demonstrations appear attractive theoretically while contributing little observational information. The observation layer therefore measures the visibility of the domain.
Definition 3.14.12.22 (Observational Yield)
Let
Obs(D)
denote the collection of distinct registered observational categories generated by D. The observational yield of D is the richness of the observable information architecture.
Consequence
Demonstrations possessing richer observation architectures generally contribute more evidence to future reconstruction efforts.
Definition 3.14.12.23 (Predictive Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Pᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of prediction classes that may be prospectively registered within the domain. Examples include:
recovery predictions,
obstruction predictions,
collapse predictions,
resilience predictions,
representation predictions,
legitimacy predictions,
trajectory predictions.
Interpretation
The predictive layer answers the question:
What can be predicted before outcomes occur?
Some domains permit only simple predictive claims. Others permit rich prospective prediction architectures.
Definition 3.14.12.24 (Predictive Breadth)
The predictive breadth of D is the number of distinct prediction families that admit prospective registration.
Consequence
Domains with larger predictive breadth contribute more opportunities for prospective testing.
Definition 3.14.12.25 (Validation Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Vᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of prospectively falsifiable claims that may be evaluated through the demonstration.
Interpretation
The validation layer answers:
What claims can actually be supported, contradicted, or left unresolved?
This is one of the most important consequence layers because the objective of the demonstration program is the generation of evidence.
Definition 3.14.12.26 (Validation Resolution)
A demonstration possesses validation resolution if outcomes permit meaningful discrimination between:
supported claims,
contradicted claims,
unresolved claims.
Consequence
Domains with poor validation resolution contribute little prospective evidence regardless of observational richness.
Definition 3.14.12.27 (Reachability Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Rᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of future compatibility structures whose existence, absence, expansion, contraction, or accessibility may become observable.
Interpretation
The reachability layer answers:
What future compatibility evidence becomes available?
Examples include:
previously unknown future pathways,
previously unknown obstructions,
latent diversity structures,
alternative realization pathways,
future-optionality architectures.
Consequence
Reachability consequences reveal information about the future landscape rather than merely about realized outcomes.
Definition 3.14.12.28 (Recovery Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Recᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of hidden recoverability claims that may be evaluated through execution of the demonstration. Examples include:
corridor existence,
selector redeployment,
pathway substitution,
unrealized compatibility,
recovery non-uniqueness.
Interpretation
The recovery layer answers:
What hidden recoverability claims become testable?
The ability to evaluate recoverability is one of the distinctive capabilities of the Compatibility–ICG architecture.
Definition 3.14.12.29 (Recovery Informational Capacity)
The recovery informational capacity of a domain measures the extent to which recovery structures may become observable.
Consequence
Domains with high recovery informational capacity provide strong opportunities for evaluating the recovery architecture developed previously.
Definition 3.14.12.30 (Pressure Consequence Architecture)
For an admissible demonstration domain D,
Prᶜ(D)
denotes the collection of pressure structures, obstruction gradients, transition tensions, and pressure accumulations that become measurable during execution of the demonstration.
Interpretation
The pressure layer answers:
Which obstruction horizons become visible?
Examples include:
pressure accumulation,
boundary thinning,
transition instability,
future-optionality contraction,
resonance degradation.
Consequence
Pressure consequences often become observable before overt failure.
Accordingly, domains possessing strong pressure visibility provide particularly useful opportunities for prospective validation of obstruction-horizon architectures.
Theorem 3.14.12.31 (Demonstration Consequence Completeness Theorem)
Let
D ∈ 𝒟*
be an admissible demonstration domain. Then every admissible contribution of D to the prospective demonstration program belongs to at least one consequence architecture contained in
ℭ(D).
Proof
Every contribution of D must arise through:
observations,
predictions,
validations,
reachability evidence,
recovery evidence,
pressure evidence.
Definitions 3.14.12.21–3.14.12.30 exhaust precisely those consequence classes. Therefore every admissible informational contribution of D belongs to at least one component architecture of ℭ(D).
∎
Corollary 3.14.12.32 (Demonstration Characterization Principle)
The value of a demonstration is determined by the informational structures it makes observable rather than by preference ordering among demonstrations.
Proof
Immediate from the Demonstration Consequence Completeness Theorem.
∎
Interpretation
The significance of the consequence architecture is methodological. The framework does not ask:
Which demonstration is best?
Instead the framework asks:
What evidence does each surviving demonstration contribute?
The output is therefore a fully characterized admissible demonstration landscape in which every surviving candidate is represented through its:
observational contributions,
predictive contributions,
validation contributions,
reachability contributions,
recovery contributions,
pressure contributions.
This preserves the admissible landscape while enabling informed selection by the researcher. The consequence architecture therefore forms the bridge between admissibility filtering and construction of the surviving demonstration landscape in the subsequent subsection.
3.14.12.6 Demonstration Comparison Architecture
The admissible demonstration landscape produced by Theorem 3.14.12.16 generally contains multiple surviving demonstration domains. The existence of multiple survivors is not a deficiency of the admissibility architecture. Rather, it is the mathematically expected consequence of an admissibility-filtering process whose purpose is elimination of inadmissible candidates rather than selection of a privileged demonstration.
Consequently, the objective of the present section is not to establish a preference ordering on admissible demonstrations. Such a construction would reintroduce the winner-selection geometry previously identified as inadmissible within the Compatibility Kernel review architecture. Instead, the objective is to characterize the informational, observational, validation, reachability, recovery, and obstruction consequences associated with each surviving admissible demonstration.
The result is a transformation from an admissible demonstration landscape into a characterized admissible demonstration landscape. Symbolically,
𝒟* → 𝒞*
where
𝒞* = { Χ(D) : D ∈ 𝒟* }.
The object 𝒞* is not a reduced landscape. No admissible demonstration is removed during characterization. Rather, the landscape acquires additional structure through explicit description of the consequences associated with each surviving domain.
The mathematical ideas employed in this section are largely established. Comparative characterization, descriptive statistics, observational capacity analysis, experimental design, and information-yield analysis all possess substantial antecedents within the broader scientific literature. The framework-specific contribution introduced here is the construction of a realization-mechanism-neutral characterization architecture for prospective demonstrations and the proof that such characterization need not induce a winner-selection relation.
Definition 3.14.12.33 (Demonstration Characterization Vector)
Let
D ∈ 𝒟*
be an admissible demonstration domain. The demonstration characterization vector associated with D is defined by
Χ(D) = (S(D), W(D), H(D), A(D), I(D), F(D))
where:
S(D) denotes the strength architecture;
W(D) denotes the weakness architecture;
H(D) denotes the validation-horizon architecture;
A(D) denotes the data-availability architecture;
I(D) denotes the information-gain architecture;
F(D) denotes the failure-risk architecture.
The collection Χ(D) is called the characterization profile of D.
Interpretation
The characterization vector is not a utility function. The characterization vector is not a ranking function. The characterization vector is not an optimization function. Most importantly, the characterization vector does not induce a preferred demonstration.
Instead, it preserves consequence structure. The vector records how a demonstration contributes evidence to the research program without compressing multiple consequences into a single scalar quantity. Thus the object of comparison is not superiority. The object of comparison is structural description.
Definition 3.14.12.34 (Characterized Demonstration Landscape)
Let
𝒟*
denote the admissible demonstration landscape. The characterized admissible demonstration landscape is
𝒞* = { Χ(D) : D ∈ 𝒟* }.
The landscape 𝒞* is obtained by enriching each admissible demonstration with its corresponding characterization profile.
Interpretation
The admissible landscape answers the question:
Which demonstrations survive filtering?
The characterized landscape answers the question:
What properties distinguish the surviving demonstrations?
The two objects are therefore distinct. The admissible landscape identifies existence. The characterized landscape identifies consequence structure.
Theorem 3.14.12.35 (Characterization Sufficiency Theorem)
Let
D ∈ 𝒟*.
Suppose all comparison-relevant structures of D are represented through:
S(D), W(D), H(D), A(D), I(D), F(D).
Then Χ(D) constitutes a sufficient characterization of D for comparative analysis within the prospective demonstration architecture.
Proof
The purpose of demonstration comparison is to determine how surviving admissible demonstrations differ with respect to future evidence production. Every such difference must arise through one or more of the following structures:
strengths of the demonstration,
weaknesses of the demonstration,
validation horizons,
data availability,
information-producing capacity,
failure-risk structures.
By assumption, these structures are represented by
S(D), W(D), H(D), A(D), I(D), F(D).
Consequently every comparison-relevant property of D appears within Χ(D). Therefore Χ(D) is sufficient for comparative characterization.
∎
Corollary 3.14.35.A (Characterization Completeness Corollary)
Every comparison-relevant distinction among admissible demonstrations must localize within at least one component of the characterization vector.
Proof
Immediate from the Characterization Sufficiency Theorem.
∎
Interpretation
